"He's still got significant swelling in his face and his eye that needs to improve," Counsell said. "But all things considered, he's in a
item.content:encoded:
CHICAGO — Cubs third baseman Alex Bregman could play again in the regular season after he sustained multiple facial fractures when he was struck in the face by a foul ball.
Chicago manager Craig Counsell said Bregman did a light workout in the weight room and tracked pitches from a machine in a batting cage. There are no plans to place him on the injured list.
"He's still got significant swelling in his face and his eye that needs to improve," Counsell said. "But all things considered, he's in a good place."
Bregman was on deck in the fourth inning of a 9-1 win at Cincinnati when he was hit on the left side of his face on Michael Busch's check-swing foul ball. Bregman immediately jogged toward the Cubs' dugout and covered his face before going back to the clubhouse with an athletic trainer.
"When everything was going down on Sunday afternoon, I think that we all thought the worst case might be a possibility," president of baseball operations Jed Hoyer said. "And all the news since then has been really good. He's had a lot of different doctor's appointments, and they've been positive. And I think we have to take it one step at a time."
Pedro Ramírez started at third in an 8-2 loss to Miami in 12 innings. He went 0 for 5 with two strikeouts. Matt Shaw also could fill in at third while Bregman is out.
Chicago (87-70) can clinch an NL wild card with a win over Miami or a loss by Arizona at Colorado.
The Cubs have five games left in the regular season. But the schedule for their weekend series at Boston is in flux because of heavy rain in the forecast.
"I think Alex is going to be fine. I really do," Counsell said. "The guy is ... he's driving home from Cincinnati and he wants to play. So he's planning on playing. He knew he had to get some good news from the doctors. He got that good news. So he's going to do everything in his power, and as long as I think symptoms don't kind of increase or happen as he increases activity, I think you're going to see him play."
Bregman is batting .262 with 26 homers and 89 RBIs in 153 games during his first season with Chicago. The three-time All-Star signed a five-year, $175 million contract with the Cubs in free agency.
The 32-year-old Bregman got off to a rough start in his new home, hitting just .229 with two homers in his first 20 games. But he has been one of Chicago's most productive players since the All-Star break, batting .305 with 17 homers and 48 RBIs in his last 57 games.
Bregman also has excelled in the postseason in the past. He won two World Series championships with the Houston Astros. He appeared in at least two postseason games in each of the previous nine years.
"To see a friend and a teammate just get hit in the face and bleeding like that is awful," Cubs second baseman Nico Hoerner said. "I think his reactions to everything has been uplifting, just him being relentlessly aggressive and positive and speaking out, all the things that he's excited to do."

item.title: [fansided.com] These Seattle Mariners won't be back after inexcusably missing the playoffs
item.dc:creator: Zachary Rotman
item.description: The Seattle Mariners were my World Series pick entering the year — that's how good I thought they'd be. Even if others weren't quite as high on them, there was every reason to believe this team could run away with a weak AL West. But that never came close to happening; in fact, just a year after making it to Game 7 of the ALCS, the Mariners will finish the 2026 campaign with a losing record and will miss the playoffs despite the American League being as weak as it's been at any point in recent m
item.content:encoded:
The Seattle Mariners were my World Series pick entering the year — that's how good I thought they'd be. Even if others weren't quite as high on them, there was every reason to believe this team could run away with a weak AL West. But that never came close to happening; in fact, just a year after making it to Game 7 of the ALCS, the Mariners will finish the 2026 campaign with a losing record and will miss the playoffs despite the American League being as weak as it's been at any point in recent memory.
Given how poorly this season went, major changes must be made to get this Mariners team back on track. Those changes begin with letting certain individuals depart after the year, starting with the most obvious one of all: manager Dan Wilson.
Manager Dan Wilson
Blaming the manager for things that have gone awry is often the easy way out, but what else can we do? On paper, the Mariners have one of the most loaded rosters in the sport, yet it feels like just about everyone has underperformed. Sure, a lot of the blame should be placed on the likes of Cal Raleigh, Julio Rodriguez, George Kirby and others who didn't do their jobs, but if everyone is failing to live up to expectations, there has to be something else going on, no?
Even if not, Wilson's lineup and bullpen management have been highly suspect dating back to his refusal to use Andres Munoz in the biggest moment of last year's ALCS decider. Wilson isn't the only reason why the Mariners are where they are, but he certainly hasn't helped them either. Again, major changes must be made, and the easiest move to start with would be letting Wilson go.
OF Taylor Ward
One move the Mariners tried to make to jumpstart their offense was trading for Taylor Ward, who, despite a down year in the power department, had an impressive .383 on-base percentage with the Baltimore Orioles prior to the trade deadline. Ward was drawing tons of walks and was essentially brought in as a table-setter for the likes of Randy Arozarena and Dominic Canzone. Unfortunately, Ward has been one of the worst hitters in the sport since the trade, going 9-for-85 (.106 BA) with one extra-base hit and no home runs. Ward's 15 wRC+ since the deadline ranks 269th out of 270 position players with at least 90 plate appearances in that span.
It's honestly a bit surprising that Ward hasn't been DFA'd to this point, but given the fact that he's a free agent after the year, it'd be stunning if Seattle even considered bringing him back. Sometimes, fits just don't work out as hoped, and this is one of those examples.
OF Victor Robles
Speaking of disappointing right-handed outfielders, what about Victor Robles? Not too long ago the Mariners had seemingly unlocked the best in Robles, who was one of their best players down the stretch of the 2024 campaign, but 2025 was a lost year for him, and 2026 went just as poorly.
Robles is slashing .256/.315/.308 with zero home runs in 65 games. Despite receiving 149 plate appearances, he has a grand total of five extra-base hits. Robles is still a decent defensive outfielder and offers a lot of speed, but he has a sub-.700 OPS against lefties and just hasn't hit enough to justify keeping around, even with one more year of club control.
SS/3B J.P. Crawford
J.P. Crawford is wrapping up his eighth season with the Mariners, and he's been a linchpin at the top of their lineup for most of those years. Crawford has always drawn a ton of walks, and his 13.3 percent walk rate this season places him in the 93rd percentile according to Baseball Savant. Unfortunately, Crawford doesn't hit for a very high average, doesn't hit for much power, doesn't offer much speed and is arguably the worst defensive shortstop in the sport.
For those reasons, is he really worth bringing back? Colt Emerson did struggle in his first taste of big-league action, but he was considered one of the best prospects in the sport and received a hefty pre-debut extension from the Mariners for a reason. He should be the shortstop on Opening Day 2027, and while Crawford could technically slide over to the hot corner, the team would benefit from finding an offensive upgrade at that position. Crawford was a great Mariner, but letting him walk in free agency feels like an easy choice.
RHP Bryce Miller
The Mariners considered trading either Bryce Miller or George Kirby at the trade deadline in their pursuit of adding a big bat to their lineup, and while they wound up settling on a rather Luis Castillo deal instead, there's no reason to believe talks won't heat up again this winter. At the end of the day, Seattle needs a game-changing bat, and they have a ton of pitching to offer up.
Logan Gilbert and Bryan Woo, their best starters, should be untouchable. The same goes for top prospect Kade Anderson. Kirby could get dealt, but his impeccable command makes him hard to part with. The Mariners could trade a Minor Leaguer like Ryan Sloan, but his upside is so massive that they'd probably shy away from doing so. That makes Miller, a pitcher with three more years of cheap club control and a very high ceiling, the likeliest choice to go. The Mariners shouldn't want to trade Miller, but given the free agent market's lack of high-end options and their starting pitching depth, a Miller trade for a middle-of-the-order bat makes too much sense.
OF Randy Arozarena
Randy Arozarena is one of the few Mariners players who actually surpassed expectations this season. He's slashing .279/.379/.480 with 26 home runs, 76 RBI and 24 stolen bases entering Wednesday's action. He's even scored an AL-leading 106 runs, which, given Seattle's brutal offense behind him, is pretty impressive. He's a player the Mariners should want back, but will he actually be back?
Arozarena is set to hit the open market this offseason, and with the kind of year he's had, he might be the best position player on the market. That reality will likely result in Arozarena receiving a ton of interest on the open market, and are we sure the Mariners will be outbidding teams in major markets? Letting Arozarena go would be an incredibly disappointing outcome, but the likely one nonetheless. The trade market is likely where they'll pursue their big bat.

item.title: [thereporteronline.com] Milestone strikeout a moment to reflect for Phillies’ Zack Wheeler
item.dc:creator: Matthew DeGeorge
item.description: PHILADELPHIA — Zack Wheeler expressed, on one hand, surety Tuesday night. On the other, genuine surprise and gratitude. Of course, the Phillies right-handed starter went into the game against Milwaukee knowing he was on 1,997 career strikeouts. item.content:encoded:
PHILADELPHIA — Zack Wheeler expressed, on one hand, surety Tuesday night. On the other, genuine surprise and gratitude.
Of course, the Phillies right-handed starter went into the game against Milwaukee knowing he was on 1,997 career strikeouts. He understood what it meant that only 95 pitchers in the history of baseball – and nine active – had crossed the 2,000-strikeout threshold.
But at plenty of junctures in a big-league career that started at age 23 but got derailed for two years, he never imagined he’d reach such a round number.
“It’s really cool, special,” Wheeler said after striking out 11 Brewers in a 6-4 Phillies win. “Some of the guys asked me in here, would you ever have thought? The answer is no. Getting into the league, trying to get your feet under you, trying to last, game to game early on, just trying to stay up in the big leagues and trying to figure it out was hard for me. And just being where I am now, it’s pretty special.”
The flipside to that disbelief, though, was the rock-steady assuredness that at age 36, Wheeler could get back to where he was at 35.
On Sept. 22, 2025, Wheeler went to sleep with thoracic decompression surgery scheduled for the next day, the removal of a rib relieving a circulation issue that had led to blood clots and ended his season.
He headed home 365 days later having made his 27th and likely final start of the season, three more than last year despite a delayed start to the season. He carries a 13-5 record, a 3.06 ERA and, by wins above replacement, his third-most valuable season among seven as a Phillie.
Which has to be at least a little surprising, right?
“I would expect it,” Wheeler said when asked if he would’ve been surprised to learn these were his stats a year post-surgery. “You’ve got to have that confidence. That’s all it is. It’s just confidence. It’s not anything else than that. You have to expect to be back to who you were. You’ve got to keep that mindset. If not, then who knows what’s going to go on in your head, and that can translate to you coming back and how you perform.”
How he performed Tuesday was as he has most of the season: Rock solid. He made quick work of the milestone, striking out the side in the first inning. His 310 career games to reach 2,000 strikeouts ties Felix Hernandez for the 13th-fewest in history.
He struck out the side in the second, too. With a whiff of Luis Lara to start the third, he set the Phillies franchise record. Already in his mind was the then-major league mark he watched from the dugout in New York in 2014, when Mets teammate Jacob deGrom fanned the first eight Marlins to tie the modern record set in 1986 by Houston’s Jim Deshaies. (deGrom’s bid was broken up by a single by the pitcher, former Phillies farmhand Jarred Cosart; the MLB record was re-set in 2021 when Miami’s Pablo Lopez struck out the first nine Braves he faced.)
“All I could think about was deGrom doing that when we were down in Miami back in the day, and the pitcher came up and got the bat on the ball,” he said. “So I was just trying to beat him, honestly. Once I got through that second inning, I was like, ‘All right, I’m trying to do this.’”
Wheeler’s run was broken by a groundout to third by Cooper Pratt. He retired the first nine in order before Garrett Mitchell looped a single off the glove of a backtracking Bryson Stott at third to lead off the fourth. Mitchell scored on William Contreras’s sac fly to get the Brewers within 3-1.
A lead-off single by nine-hitter David Hamilton and a walk to Jackson Chourio put two on in the sixth. Wheeler froze Brice Turang, Hamilton and Chourio stealing third and second. Contreras beat Wheeler on a first-pitch fastball that was a little too low, the catcher golfing a liner just over the reach of a leaping Trea Turner at short for a two-run single and a 3-3 game, sending Wheeler to the no-decision.
“I wanted to go in, but it was down. I wanted it more up,” he said. “Down’s a little easier to hit than up. That’s probably what I was most upset about tonight, and probably the pitch I hate the most so far this season.”
There hasn’t been much to regret this year. Wheeler’s injury dealt a huge confidence blow to the Phillies heading into the postseason last year. It started him on the injured list in 2026, but he blew through the six month estimated timeline to debut by the end of April.
From that point on, he was the Zack Wheeler of old, so much so that he’s likely to start the first game of a Phillies Wild Card series despite not being one of the team’s two All-Star starters this season.
A month into his return, his ERA sat at 1.67, excluding a five-start stretch from late July to late August in which he allowed 23 earned runs in 24.1 innings around an rain-interrupted outing in Baltimore, he’s been spectacular, with an ERA of 2.05 over his other 22 starts.
Wheeler isn’t prone to reflection, especially midseason. The strikeout milestone forced a bit of it upon him. He still approached it as having one start left, though he’d only pitch in Sunday’s finale if the Phillies need it, which is highly avoidable at a magic number of 2 after Tuesday’s action.
He took the chance to express gratitude: to his wife and family, to the catchers and coaches he’s had through his 12 major league seasons. He reserved a special mention for Phillies head athletic trainer Paul Buchheit for the rehabilitation plan from last year.
The round number offered perspective, for a blue-chip prospect who was outstanding in his first two seasons more than a decade ago but then missed two full seasons with a complicated recovery from Tommy John surgery. He’s navigated the jump from New York to Philly for two big contracts, weathered changes to the expectations of the position, bridged eras from batting to designated hitters, from pitch clocks to ABS.
Through it all, Wheeler has continually dealt every fifth day, which is what a milestone like Tuesday’s fetes.
“The road was hard coming back from that,” Wheeler said of his Tommy John ordeal. “That was another point where I didn’t know what to expect because it was taking longer than what we all expected at the time. So, I was just trying to get back out there. It was kind of like starting over again, just trying to get back out there, just lasting, and I was able to figure it out.”

item.content:encoded:
Blue Jays news: Juan Soto thinks Max Scherzer 'wants to play forever.' Will he make it 20 years next season? appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
Max Scherzer has yet to reveal whether he plans to return for a 20th MLB season in 2027, but former teammate Juan Soto believes the Toronto Blue Jays veteran still has the competitive drive to keep pitching.
Scherzer, who is scheduled to make his 500th career MLB appearance Wednesday, recently declined to discuss his plans for next season. The 42-year-old has instead pointed to his ability to compete in meaningful games as the standard he uses to determine whether he should continue playing.
"You can give me a ball in a playoff start, and I can go out there and compete for it," Scherzer said last week, as reported by Brittany Ghiroli and Mitch Bannon of The Athletic. "That's my fundamental kind of litmus test of play or not play."
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
Soto, who played alongside Scherzer with the Washington Nationals and won the 2019 World Series with him, believes Scherzer's competitiveness continues to fuel him.
"I think he wants to play forever," Soto said, per Ghiroli and Bannon. "The love for the game he has, how confident he is. He's a guy who tries to win in every aspect, people don't even know, it's not even baseball. It's life.
"Everything with him is so competitive, and I think that's what drives him. It makes him go out there and try to show everybody he can still do it."
Scherzer has continued to adapt throughout the later stages of his career while maintaining a demanding workout routine between starts. His next appearance will add another milestone to a career that has included 499 games and 490 starts.
The right-hander enters Wednesday with a 224-125 career record, 3.28 ERA and 1.09 WHIP across 3,035 2/3 innings, according to datat from ESPN. He has recorded 3,543 strikeouts and 810 walks.
Scherzer has made 16 starts for Toronto this season, going 3-8 with a 6.07 ERA and 1.36 WHIP over 72 2/3 innings. He has struck out 54 and walked 31.
His most recent start provided a better result. Scherzer allowed one run on three hits over five innings in Toronto's 5-1 win over the Detroit Tigers on Sept. 16, earning his second win in four starts. He walked three and struck out three as the Blue Jays ended Detroit's six-game winning streak.
Reporting by Ian Harrison of The Associated Press contributed to this article.
Related: Blue Jays playoff hopes on pause after Orioles postponement

item.content:encoded:
The Toronto Blue Jays are in the middle of a three-game series against the Baltimore Orioles.
The Orioles won the first game of the series 4-3 on Monday. Game 2 was postponed due to inclement weather, and the series will finish with a doubleheader on Wednesday.
The first game of the doubleheader is scheduled to start at 1:35 p.m. EDT. The second game will begin at 6:35 p.m. EDT.
The Blue Jays announced their lineup for the first game of the doubleheader, and it includes a notable decision involving Vladimir Guerrero Jr.
Toronto Blue Jays Make Vladimir Guerrero Jr. Decision Amid Orioles Series
Guerrero is out of the lineup for the second straight game for the first game of the doubleheader on Wednesday.
The first baseman was removed from Sunday’s win over the Texas Rangers with lower back tightness, according to MLB.com’s Keegan Matheson.
Update: Guerrero is now IN the lineup.
Here is Toronto’s lineup for Wednesday afternoon’s game:
- Nathan Lukes RF
- Vladimir Guerrero Jr. 1B
- Kazuma Okamoto 3B
- George Springer DH
- Josh Smith LF
- Andres Gimenez SS
- Brandon Valenzuela C
- Myles Straw CF
- Ernie Clement 2B
SP: RHP Max Scherzer (3-8, 6.07 ERA, 54 SO)
Here is the Orioles’ lineup:
- Dylan Beavers LF
- Pete Alonso 1B
- Gunnar Henderson SS
- Coby Mayo DH
- Edwin Encarnacion-Strand 3B
- Colton Cowser CF
- Jeremiah Jackson 2B
- Leody Taveras RF
- Carlos Narvaez C
SP: RHP Chris Bassitt (8-5, 4.64 ERA, 72 SO)
Looking at Vladimir Guerrero Jr.’s Season
Guerrero has easily had the worst season of his career, posting 1.2 fWAR and a 97 wRC+ with just nine home runs and 56 RBI over 141 games.
In Guerrero’s defense, he has dealt with numerous injuries this year that he played through. His back has bothered him much of the season, and he also dealt with a hamstring issue earlier this season. Not to mention, he missed games with a concussion.
Since making his MLB debut in 2019, Guerrero has posted 21.8 fWAR and a 132 wRC+ with 192 home runs and 647 RBI. The first baseman signed a 14-year, $500 million contract extension with Toronto in spring 2025.
Toronto Blue Jays Right Now
One year after making it to the World Series, Toronto has a 77-80 record.
The Blue Jays haven’t been officially eliminated yet, but just one more loss from the club will seal their fate.
Even if they win out, they’d need a ton of help from around the league to sneak into the playoffs.

item.title: [Diario AS] Dylan Cease opened up on his Cy Young hopes before Blue Jays ace suffered shoulder scare
item.dc:creator: Jennifer Bubel
item.description: Dylan Cease has spent much of his first season with the Toronto Blue Jays in the Cy Young conversation, and the right-hander made it clear that winning the award would mean a lot to him. In an interview conducted by Alex Withers on behalf of Casino.org Canada and made available to AS, before his recent shoulder scare, Cease said: “Obviously, winning a Cy Young is an amazing accomplishment. I think any pitcher would be over the moon to win one and the same goes for me.” Those comments have a diff
item.content:encoded:
Dylan Cease has spent much of his first season with the Toronto Blue Jays in the Cy Young conversation, and the right-hander made it clear that winning the award would mean a lot to him.
In an interview conducted by Alex Withers on behalf of Casino.org Canada and made available to AS, before his recent shoulder scare, Cease said: “Obviously, winning a Cy Young is an amazing accomplishment. I think any pitcher would be over the moon to win one and the same goes for me.”
Those comments have a different impact now that Cease’s season was suddenly thrown into uncertainty. The Blue Jays sent their ace for an MRI after his September 18 start against the Texas Rangers, when his velocity dipped and he lasted just 2⅔ innings in a 7-1 Toronto loss. The MRI revealed inflammation in his right shoulder but no structural damage, so he will not need surgery.
Dylan Cease says that his shoulder MRI revealed inflammation.
Cease described his shoulder as “heavy and achy.” pic.twitter.com/TpEXebtrWf
He has not been ruled out from pitching again this season, although his availability for Toronto’s final series against the Cincinnati Reds remains uncertain.
Dylan Cease has put together a Cy Young-caliber season
Whatever happens with the award, Cease has put together one of the best seasons of his career. The 30-year-old has gone 11-6 with a 2.40 ERA and 1.10 WHIP across 29 starts. His 239 strikeouts lead the American League, while he has thrown 169 innings. That production has made Cease one of the leading names in the American League Cy Young discussion during his first season in Toronto.
A NEW single-season career-high for Cease! #BlueJays50 pic.twitter.com/C2aUUiUmLW
— Toronto Blue Jays (@BlueJays) September 13, 2026
The right-hander said one of the reasons he has been satisfied with his campaign is the consistency of his execution.
“I think the biggest thing that’s making me confident in myself is that I’ve only had a handful of starts where I’ve left feeling really disappointed,” Cease said. “I feel like I’ve executed well. Even in the games where I haven’t really had my best stuff or command, I’ve been able to mix well enough and get the job done.”
Cease has struck out 34.9 percent of the batters he has faced this season and has posted a 2.55 FIP, according to StatMuse.
On the bright side, atleast the Jays found some absolute studs this season
Spencer Miles, Dylan Cease, Big Oak, Brett Bateman, etc…
All those dudes are locked up for TIME and are absolutely part of the solution moving forward pic.twitter.com/I7pRirkg0C
What changed for Dylan Cease in 2026?
Cease was also asked what he believed had made the biggest difference in taking his pitching to another level this season. His answer was relatively simple: diversification.
“I think the pitch mix and diversifying my pitch mix more has really helped me kick on,” Cease said.
The Blue Jays’ ace also pointed to a change in his mental approach to pitching.
“You know, turning my head and my eyes off the target briefly,” he said. “That’s all given me a really good feel for my game and performance.”
All of this has helped Cease navigate starts even when he hasn’t had his best command or pure stuff, something he specifically cited when evaluating his season. It has also allowed him to remain effective despite a difficult September.
Cease’s final September outing before his shoulder issue was his roughest of the season. He allowed four runs, three hits, and six walks in 2⅔ innings against Texas, with the six walks representing a season high. His average fastball velocity in the outing dropped to 93.6 mph, according to Sportsnet.
Dylan Cease pitched 2.2 innings in Texas tonight, his shortest outing of the season
He allowed one earned run on three hits and a season-high six walks, but a Blue Jays error resulted in three unearned runs pic.twitter.com/34yYIK4i48
Dylan Cease’s shoulder issue leaves his season in limbo
The drop in velocity prompted the Blue Jays to send Cease back to Toronto for imaging. That’s when they figured out he wouldn’t need surgery, but his pitching is still uncertain for the rest of the season. And with Cease otherwise in position for one of baseball’s biggest individual honors, the timing is quite unfortunate.
Cease signed a seven-year, $210 million contract with the Blue Jays last December and has been a central part of a rotation that has dealt with a long list of injuries throughout the season. Now, rather than simply focusing on where he might finish in the Cy Young voting, Toronto has to wait and see whether its ace can return for the final series of the regular season.

item.title: [FanSided] MLB Rumors: Marcelo Mayer's Red Sox anger and Don Mattingly's Phillies future
item.dc:creator: Chris Landers
item.description: It's not the trade that will have the most bearing on who wins the World Series this fall, but the Boston Red Sox' decision to dump former top prospect Marcelo Mayer onto the San Francisco Giants stands out as among the most quietly curious of this past deadline. Then again, hearing Mayer and his family speak about his time in Boston ahead of his debut with his new team, perhaps it was for the best all the way around. Will Mayer be able to prove that the Red Sox got this one wrong? The latest ro
item.content:encoded:
It's not the trade that will have the most bearing on who wins the World Series this fall, but the Boston Red Sox' decision to dump former top prospect Marcelo Mayer onto the San Francisco Giants stands out as among the most quietly curious of this past deadline. Then again, hearing Mayer and his family speak about his time in Boston ahead of his debut with his new team, perhaps it was for the best all the way around.
Will Mayer be able to prove that the Red Sox got this one wrong? The latest round of MLB rumors has more on that as well as the Philadelphia Phillies' looming Don Mattingly decision and Alex Bregman on the mend for the Chicago Cubs.
Marcelo Mayer and his family sound relieved to be out of Boston
Not all that long ago, Mayer was a crucial part of the future for the Red Sox, as much a foundational prospect as Roman Anthony. But he struggled to stay healthy over the last two years, and struggled to hit even when he was in the lineup. Eventually, Boston decided they'd seen enough, flipping the young infielder to San Francisco at this year's trade deadline — and it seems as though Mayer is eager to prove that Craig Breslow was wrong to cut bait.
According to Susan Slusser of the San Francisco Chronicle, Mayer and his family "let the Red Sox front office know they'd be comfortable with a trade" as the atmosphere in Boston grew hostile toward the 23-year-old.
“Obviously, it didn’t go the way I wanted,” Mayer told Slusser, “and obviously, outside the lines, it’s a lot over there.”
Mayer's dad was willing to go even further, saying that he "jumped 30 feet in the air" when he heard the news that his son was headed back to his home state of California.
On the one hand, Mayer's offensive numbers over his first two big-league seasons are undeniably ugly, and he's missed time due to injury in each of the past four years. Then again, none those health issues seem to be of the chronic variety, and they undoubtedly hampered his development. You can understand why the Red Sox weren't willing to wait around for Mayer to maybe turn into a big-league second baseman, but you can also understand why the Giants were eager to give him a second chance — and why, given all the criticism he faced from fans and talk-radio types in Boston about whether he was soft, Mayer can't wait to get back on the field.
Phillies waiting until offseason to make a decision about Don Mattingly
It's been a big few days for interim managers, with both Chad Tracy in Boston and Andy Green with the Mets earning the full-time job moving forward. But no such vote of confidence has come for Phillies interim skipper Don Mattingly, who took over from Rob Thomson back in late April and has guided the team to the brink of a Wild Card spot. And from the sound of it, he shouldn't get his hopes up.
"[We] have felt it is better to wait until our season is complete," Phillies president Dave Dombrowski told reporters this week, per Scott Lauber of the Inquirer.
That seems to be a pretty clear warning: Take this team deep into October, or else. And really, despite Mattingly's 78-51 record at the helm this season, it's hard to fault Dombrowski too much here. The roster Mattingly inherited certainly has its flaws, with a thin bullpen and a lineup with multiple trouble spots. But Mattingly also hasn't helped matters at times, with some questionable decision-making that makes clear why his previous managerial stints ended unhappily.
Yes, he deserves credit for his role in Philly's turnaround. But it has much more to do with the players on the field than anything else, and the Phillies are wise not to tie themselves to a 65-year-old who could very well come back to bite the team in the postseason. And if Mattingly does prove himself next month, they can very easily revisit the matter.
Cubs appear to have dodged a bullet with Alex Bregman injury
The Cubs suffered a real scare in Cincinnati over the weekend, when star third baseman Alex Bregman took a line drive directly to the face while standing in the on-deck circle. Given the frightening nature of the injury and the timing just a week before the end of the regular season, it was hard not to fear that Chicago might have to at least begin its playoff journey without a guy who's been one of their very best players in the second half.
Thankfully, though, the Cubs appear to have gotten good news. Bregman suffered multiple facial fractures in the incident, but manager Craig Counsell told reporters on Tuesday that the veteran isn't expected to go on the IL — and that he might even be able to return to the lineup before the regular season concludes.
Will Bregman be the same guy he was prior to the injury? That remains to be seen. But as things stand right now, it seems like he'll at the very least be ready to go for the Cubs' first postseason game next week, and that's a huge sigh of relief.

item.dc:creator: Caleb Kerney
item.description: The Toronto Blue Jays playoff hopes hang by a thread. That thread will face a razor-sharp challenge in a Baltimore Orioles double-header. However, the other Blue Jays news of the day involves Brandon Valenzuela. The first game of their doubleheader involves Max Scherzer taking the mound for the Blue Jays. He will go up against Chris Bassitt at 11:35 AM Mountain Time, 1:35 PM Eastern Time. Toronto Blue Jays News: Brandon Valenzuela In, Alejandro Kirk Out For Game 1 Against The Baltimore Orioles P
item.content:encoded:
The Toronto Blue Jays playoff hopes hang by a thread. That thread will face a razor-sharp challenge in a Baltimore Orioles double-header. However, the other Blue Jays news of the day involves Brandon Valenzuela.
The first game of their doubleheader involves Max Scherzer taking the mound for the Blue Jays. He will go up against Chris Bassitt at 11:35 AM Mountain Time, 1:35 PM Eastern Time.
Toronto Blue Jays News: Brandon Valenzuela In, Alejandro Kirk Out For Game 1 Against The Baltimore Orioles
Prior to the first pitch of today’s doubleheader, the Blue Jays announced their lineup. That lineup marks Valenzuela’s return.
Here is the lineup that the Blue Jays announced:
- RF: Nathan Lukes
- LF: Josh Smith
- 3B: Kazuma Okamoto
- DH: George Springer
- 1B: Sean Keys
- SS: Andres Gimenez
- C: Brandon Valenzuela
- CF: Myles Straw
- 2B: Ernie Clement
Starting Pitcher: Max Scherzer.
“Let’s play TWO! #BlueJays50,” the team announced.
This lineup obviously includes Valenzuela in addition to Myles Straw. The 25-year-old is coming in for Alejandro Kirk, who is coming out. Brett Bateman is missing the game due to injury.
Looking At Brandon Valenzuela
Valenzuela and Kirk have been sharing home plate all season. Between injuries and hot/cold play, it hasn’t been that difficult for John Schneider to shuffle the deck once in a while.
Valenzuela was first acquired by the Blue Jays in July 2025.
“OFFICIAL: We’ve acquired C Brandon Valenzuela from the Padres in exchange for INF Will Wagner. Welcome to our Blue Jays family!” the team announced over a year ago.
Valenzuela played 26 games with the Buffalo Bisons after his acquisition last year. In those games, he recorded 19 hits, six doubles, 12 RBIs, and three home runs.
Fast forward to this season, and Valenzuela has 51 hits, nine doubles, two stolen bases, 21 RBIs, and eight home runs in 88 games.
Looking at Alejandro Kirk
Of all the things that have been going wrong lately, Kirk has been one of the things going right.
The 27-year-old has nine hits, six RBIs, and one home run in his last seven games. In those games, Kirk has a .346 batting average and a .433 on-base percentage.
With these two behind the plate for the Blue Jays for the foreseeable future, Toronto will be well taken care of.

item.content:encoded:
Sixteen MLB games are on the board for Wednesday, September 23, and Eric Lindquist is treating it like the calendar demands: light on volume, heavier on conviction. "Not a lot of volume, quite a few plays," he said early in the show, and with the playoffs bearing down and lines already moving overnight, he picked his spots across the full board rather than forcing something in every window. He came into the day up slightly after a Tuesday that leaned on a PrizePicks card headlined by Mickey Moniac's home run at plus-475, and he's carrying that same selectivity into Wednesday: seven official plays, a handful of leans he never turned into bets, and a lot of games he talked through and walked away from entirely.
Mike Trout — Lindy's one MLB home run swing on today's board.
The Quick Answer
Lindy's Wednesday, September 23 card has seven official plays: Mike Trout (LAA) to hit a home run against left-hander Jeffrey Springs at plus-350, Toronto's moneyline in the bullpen-game second half of their Baltimore doubleheader at minus-108, Philadelphia's moneyline against Milwaukee at plus-124, the under 7.5 total for Cardinals-Pirates at even money, the over 8.5 total for White Sox-Royals at minus-107, Foster Griffin (CLE) for 5-plus strikeouts against a watered-down Red Sox lineup, and the Dodgers' moneyline against San Francisco in a "coin-flippy" spot with Yamamoto on the mound. Beyond that card, he talked through moneyline leans on Houston and the Yankees that never became bets, and passed on several other games entirely. The full breakdown is below.
Watch The Video
Lindy built this card live on the OddsShopper channel, working through all 16 MLB games before settling on the seven plays below. If you'd rather shop these numbers yourself while you watch, OddsShopper Pro is free to try for 7 days.
The Plays At A Glance
| The Play | The market | The size |
|---|---|---|
| Mike Trout (LAA) | To hit a home run vs. Jeffrey Springs | His one home run swing of the day |
| Toronto Blue Jays | Moneyline, Game 2 of the Baltimore doubleheader | Not specified |
| Philadelphia Phillies | Moneyline vs. Milwaukee (+124) | A half unit |
| Cardinals-Pirates | Under 7.5 (even money) | Not specified |
| White Sox-Royals | Over 8.5 (-107) | 0.3 units |
| Foster Griffin (CLE) | 5+ strikeouts vs. Boston | A quarter unit |
| Los Angeles Dodgers | Moneyline vs. San Francisco | A quarter unit |
Seven plays spread across seven different games, and a common thread runs through them: none of them lean on chasing a hot lineup. They're built on pitching matchups, park and weather notes, and one hitter the market has priced wrong.
His Home Run Play: Mike Trout Against A Lefty Who Can't Miss Bats
Lindy called this "an interesting one" the moment he got to it, and he was upfront that his own history with Mike Trout hasn't been profitable. But the numbers here pulled him in anyway. Trout is running a .221 expected ISO against left-handed pitching this year against just a .157 realized mark, a gap Lindy pointed to directly as evidence he's been unlucky rather than declining. Trout also strikes out at a sub-20% clip against left-handers, which matters against Jeffrey Springs, a southpaw Lindy said has "given up crazy boatloads of power to lefties and righties alike" this season. The Angels don't have much protection behind Trout from the left side of the plate, either. Lindy singled out Zach Neto as the only other left-handed bat he trusts in that lineup, and even called his price short. Mike Trout (LAA) to hit a home run against Jeffrey Springs, priced at plus-350 when Lindy made the call and sitting at plus-326 as of this recording, his only home run swing on a board that was mostly barren for the long ball.
Toronto Moneyline: The Bullpen Game Angle
The Blue Jays and Orioles are playing a doubleheader to make up a Tuesday rainout, and Lindy split his read on the two games. In the opener, he weighed Max Scherzer against Chris Bassett and talked himself out of the Toronto side, calling it "much closer" than the market had it and passing entirely. The second game is where he landed: Toronto is running a true bullpen game behind reliever CJ Van, while Baltimore hands the ball to Trey Gibson with the clear goal of eating innings before the season ends. Both teams are out of contention and playing out the string, but Lindy still liked Toronto's moneyline in Game 2 at minus-108, noting it was surprising to see the price sit that close given the bullpen-game context.
Phillies Moneyline: Nola At Home, A Good Park For Lefty Power
Milwaukee sends Logan Henderson, a strikeout-heavy arm, into Philadelphia while the Brewers are trying to hold off the Dodgers for the top seed in the National League. Lindy's read is that Citizens Bank Park is exactly the wrong park for that matchup to play out cleanly, given how well it treats left-handed power, and he noted Aaron Nola has pitched much better at home over the past month with pronounced home-road splits in his favor. Philadelphia's moneyline at plus-124, sized at a half unit, smaller than his usual game-line play, but not one he skipped.
Cardinals-Pirates: Betting The Weather, Not The Names
This one came down to conditions more than personnel. Wind blowing in at 12-13 mph at PNC Park is, in Lindy's words, "very advantageous pitching weather," and he wasn't even certain who'd be on the mound behind the Pirates' starter given how unsettled that staff has looked. Matthew Liberatore gets the ball for St. Louis, and Lindy flagged that Liberatore's pitch counts in his last three outings (72, 69, 81) suggest he could be in line for regression at some point. Just not, in his view, on a cold, wind-in night at a pitcher's park. Under 7.5 at even money, his second play built around ballpark conditions on this card.
White Sox-Royals: A Total Built On A Shaky Chicago Arm
Lindy was blunt about this one, flatly calling White Sox right-hander Eric Fedde horrible, and he's not buying into him regardless of the platoon matchup. Seth Lugo gets the ball for a Kansas City club Lindy still expects to run out a competitive lineup. With both bullpens likely to see plenty of work behind shaky starting pitching, he landed on the total. Over 8.5 at minus-107, sized at 0.3 units, one of his smaller plays on the card, but one he called "an all right spot to dip your toes into."
Foster Griffin Strikeouts: A Lineup With Nothing Left To Play For
Cleveland still has real playoff stakes; Boston's season, in Lindy's words, is "completely done," with the Red Sox locked into their wild-card spot with nothing left to jockey for. That combination is why he's not expecting Boston's best everyday lineup on the field, and it's the setup behind his smallest play of the day. Foster Griffin (CLE) for 5-plus strikeouts, sized at just a quarter unit. Griffin's 14.5 outs-recorded prop got a look too; Lindy leaned the over but called the hold on that number too heavy to bet, so it stayed off the card.
Dodgers Moneyline: A Coin Flip With Ohtani Coming Back
Yoshinobu Yamamoto got bumped up to start Wednesday for Los Angeles after the Dodgers ran a bullpen game against San Francisco and Robbie Ray, and Lindy's read leans on two things: Los Angeles needs innings out of Yamamoto with no days off left in the schedule, and Shohei Ohtani is expected back atop the lineup after his bicep issue. The Dodgers are chasing Milwaukee for the top seed in the National League, which means a full night of scoreboard-watching alongside their own game. The price is "closer to coin-flippy," in Lindy's words, and he stopped short of a big stand, but he still landed on it. Los Angeles Dodgers moneyline against San Francisco, sized at a quarter unit.
Leans He Didn't Fire
Two more spots got real analysis without becoming plays, and the LEAN ≠ PLAY line matters here. Lindy called Houston's moneyline against Seattle "probably the closest play I've got here on a lean section" given George Kirby's fading strikeout stuff and Houston's clear edge in stakes, but he stopped short of actually betting it. The Yankees' moneyline against Tampa Bay at minus-157 got a similar treatment: Lindy reasoned that a watered-down Rays lineup the day after clinching the AL East justifies the price even with the extra juice, but he flagged the number as more than he'd normally pay, so it stays a lean rather than a confirmed play. A thinner look at Minnesota's moneyline against a struggling Giants lineup also never got a price attached or a firm commitment.
Games He Passed On Entirely
Several more games got attention and no play. A pitcher's matchup drawing a righty-heavy Washington lineup fronted by CJ Abrams got a look, but Lindy said he didn't need to force a bet on that game. The Reds-Braves game drew a lean toward the under on Chris Sale's inflated strikeout total, but Lindy said the whole game was "very tough to bet" and left it alone. Arizona's game in Colorado got a long look given the Diamondbacks' playoff push, but nothing concrete came of it. A Nico Hoerner-centered look at the Marlins-Cubs game also stayed analysis only, and Lindy said he might add a Nolan McLean strikeout prop for the Mets-Rangers game later once he finished running his numbers overnight; it wasn't locked in at the time of recording.
Start Your Free Trial
Lindy's card today is a reminder that a full board doesn't mean a full bet card: seven plays out of 16 games, each built on a specific pitching, park, or matchup edge rather than a hot lineup. OddsShopper checks every book at once and de-vigs the market to a fair price, the same math behind gaps like the one between Trout's plus-350 call and where the market has since settled.

You can also shop the live board yourself at the OddsShopper MLB odds screen, check FanDuel's current offer — how to claim it, or use our free bet converter if a sportsbook credits you a bonus bet off Wednesday's action. For more home run swings across the rest of the board, see our MLB home run picks hub, and our guide to finding +EV bets walks through the de-vig math behind Lindy's Trout read.
FAQ
Who Is Lindy And Where Can I Follow His MLB Picks?
Lindy is Eric Lindquist, who hosts "Lindy's Leans, Likes & Locks" on the OddsShopper channel and posts his full daily card on Tails.
What Was Lindy's Biggest Play On The Wednesday, September 23 Card?
His headline play was Mike Trout (LAA) to hit a home run against left-hander Jeffrey Springs at plus-350. He backed it with six more official plays: Toronto's moneyline in Game 2 of their Baltimore doubleheader, Philadelphia's moneyline against Milwaukee, the under on Cardinals-Pirates, the over on White Sox-Royals, a Foster Griffin strikeout prop, and the Dodgers' moneyline against San Francisco.
Does A Lean Count The Same As An Official Play?
No. Lindy talks through spots he's watching but hasn't bet, like Wednesday's Houston and Yankees moneyline leans, separately from the plays he's actually on. This recap only credits him with the seven he officially fired.
This recap covers Eric Lindquist's official plays from the Wednesday, September 23 "Lindy's Leans, Likes & Locks" show; follow his full card on Tails. Bets are opinions, not guarantees. Please gamble responsibly, 21+.

item.content:encoded:
Sep 23, 2026, 11:45 AM ET
Toronto Blue Jays first baseman Vladimir Guerrero Jr. (back) remains out of action for Game 1 of Wednesday's doubleheader at Camden Yards against the division-rival Baltimore Orioles, per MLB.com. Sean Keys will make another start at first base and will bat fifth against Orioles right-hander Chris Bassitt. Guerrero is considered day-to-day right now in the final week of the regular season after departing Sunday's game early against the Texas Rangers due to tightness in his lower back. It is something that the 27-year-old Canadian slugger has already dealt with this year, and it could explain why the six-time All-Star has had a very disappointing 2026 campaign. Guerrero enters play on Wednesday with a .263/.336/.359 slash line, a .695 OPS, only nine home runs, 56 RBI, 71 runs scored, and seven steals across his 529 at-bats. Toronto entered play on Wednesday four games out of the final wild-card spot in the American League and on the brink of elimination. If they lose the first game of Wednesday's doubleheader, Guerrero could be shut down for the rest of the week.--Keith Hernandez
Source: MLB.com
More Recent News
Jeremy Pena Suffers Wrist Injury on Tuesday


Keith Hernandez




Sep 23, 2026, 11:38 AM ET
Houston Astros shortstop Jeremy Pena (wrist) was hit on the right wrist with a 96.4 mph sinker in Tuesday's game against the Seattle Mariners and was removed in the eighth inning, according to Chandler Rome of The Athletic. Pena attempted to stay in the contest, but he was eventually replaced by Nick Allen at shortstop after going 1-for-4 at the plate with two runs scored and two strikeouts. The Astros likely sent Pena for X-rays, and we will pass along the results when we have them. Fantasy managers will want to check back later to see if the Astros' starting shortstop will be available for Wednesday's game in Seattle against the Mariners. Losing Pena for the rest of the final week of the 2026 regular season would be a huge blow, with the Astros going into Wednesday's action tied for first in the American League West with the Texas Rangers. The 29-year-old Pena has missed time this year due to various injuries, but he has been solid when healthy, slashing .275/.325/.469 with a .795 OPS, 20 home runs, 51 RBI, 77 runs scored, and 10 stolen bases in 107 games across 461 plate appearances.--Keith Hernandez
Source: The Athletic - Chandler Rome
Ceddanne Rafaela Set to Return From Injured List on Wednesday


Keith Hernandez




Sep 22, 2026, 11:08 PM ET
The Boston Red Sox plan to activate second baseman/outfielder Ceddanne Rafaela (quadriceps) from the 10-day injured list on Wednesday, manager Chad Tracy told Tim Healey of The Boston Globe. Rafaela should be back in the starting lineup for Boston in Game 2 of the series against the Cleveland Guardians. He has been out since Sept. 6 with a strained right quad but did not play in a minor-league rehab game. The 26-year-old continues to contribute across most fantasy baseball categories, but he could be a little rusty upon his return to the big leagues as the Red Sox try to get him going again before the wild-card series against the division-rival New York Yankees begins next week. Rafaela made the All-Star team for the first time in his career in 2026 and will return to a nice .282/.317/.443 slash line, a career-high .760 OPS, 16 home runs, 70 RBI, 17 stolen bases, and 67 runs scored across 135 games played. If Rafaela hits a home run by the end of the weekend, he will have a new career high in home runs in his fourth year in the majors.--Keith Hernandez

However, the right-hander's production upside is limited by his middling strikeout rate (21.8%) and his poor walk rate (11.4%). item.title: [The Times of India] Meet Julio Rodriguez’s alter ego ‘DJ Pleno’: How the Seattle Mariners star is building a surprising second identity through house music, live sets and his growing passion for DJing
item.dc:creator: Global Sports Desk
item.description: Seattle Mariners center fielder Julio Rodriguez is one of the most recognisable young faces in Major League Baseball with his energetic personality and impact on the field. But by 2026, Rodriguez is starting to be known for another facet of himself as he delves into music and live DJ sets. She goes by 'DJ Pleno' behind the turntables and is 25 years old. It’s a different identity from his baseball career, allowing Rodriguez to tinker with something that doesn’t have anything to do with the No. 4
item.content:encoded:
Seattle Mariners center fielder Julio Rodriguez is one of the most recognisable young faces in Major League Baseball with his energetic personality and impact on the field. But by 2026, Rodriguez is starting to be known for another facet of himself as he delves into music and live DJ sets.
She goes by 'DJ Pleno' behind the turntables and is 25 years old. It’s a different identity from his baseball career, allowing Rodriguez to tinker with something that doesn’t have anything to do with the No. 44 jersey or his duties as a Mariners star. What began as a simple turntable in his home has now become a hobby that he wants to continue to build on.
MLB star Julio Rodriguez introduces Seattle Mariners fans to DJ Pleno
Rodriguez’s DJ persona morphed from a private hobby to a public performance on August 7, 2026, at T-Mobile Park during the Seattle Mariners’ Alumni Home Run Derby. The event was part of the organization’s 50 Seasons Celebration Weekend and featured a number of former Mariners, including star attraction Ichiro Suzuki.
But while the alumni were in the home run competition, Rodriguez had a different task. The Mariners star DJed live under the 'DJ Pleno' name, bringing house music to the ballpark after the game.
The performance gave Rodriguez an opportunity to show a side of himself that most fans had not seen before.
He was no longer in the batter’s box or patrolling center field he was in charge of music and trying to create an atmosphere for the crowd.
To Rodriguez, the name 'Pleno' has meaning. The word has Spanish origins and is ultimately derived from Latin plēnus and ideas like being full, complete or fulfilled.
That meaning helped Rodriguez find an identity that didn't revolve around baseball. Instead of opting for a name that referenced his number on his jersey, the Mariners or his baseball nickname, he wanted 'DJ Pleno' to be its own thing.
The concept also reflects what Rodriguez wants to embody in the persona. He has associated the project with feeling good, being fulfilled and doing things that bring personal satisfaction in his comments around 'DJ Pleno'.
The Alumni Home Run Derby performance was a big step forward because most of Rodriguez’s previous DJing had been done away from a large crowd.
After the Mariners were knocked out of the playoffs in 2025, he began to tinker with equipment at his home in the Seattle area. His initial set-up was primitive, and Rodriguez admitted he had no idea what all the various controls on the equipment did.
His friends who had DJ experience also made fun of his early equipment and method. Rodriguez did not give up the hobby but bought more equipment and kept on practising.
How Julio Rodriguez discovered his passion for DJing
Rodriguez’s interest in DJing came during a period when he was looking for something outside of baseball. He’s been in the limelight since his teenage years, and his career has kept baseball front and center in his everyday life, from top prospect to established MLB star.
DJing gives Rodriguez a different learning experience
Rodriguez’s interest in music goes back a long way, but it was the decision to learn DJing that made it an active hobby. He bought a basic turntable and started practising at home after the 2025 season.
There was an instant learning curve. Rodriguez said he initially had difficulty understanding the controls, but repeated practice helped him become more comfortable with the equipment and the process of mixing tracks.
His musical preferences lie in house music and he is associated with artists such as Martin Garrix and Black Coffee. He doesn’t have a strict daily routine for DJing. Instead, Rodriguez likes to train when the mood is right.
There’s an interesting link to Rodriguez’s baseball career and his new hobby. He has spent most of his life working on his baseball skills, so a lot of the game comes on instinct through years of repetition.
As a novice, Rodriguez has to relearn the fundamentals, make mistakes and slowly improve. And that process has allowed him to think about his own development as a baseball player and to appreciate how much work went into getting to the major leagues.
Rodriguez has likened the thrill of having control of a DJ set to the sensation of creating a big moment on a baseball field.
If you’re a player accustomed to the decibel levels at T-Mobile Park, then playing music in front of a crowd isn’t all that foreign. The energy may be similar, but the source of attention is different.
What comes next for Julio Rodriguez and DJ Pleno
Rodriguez has described 'DJ Pleno' as a work in progress. There doesn’t seem to be a concrete, long-term business plan for the project, but the Mariners star has said he’d like to continue to grow and eventually expand what he’s able to do with music.
He wants to do more than just mix. Rodriguez has said he wants to do his own music in the future, which could see the project move from DJing to production.
Next for Rodriguez is to get more confidence technically and gain more experience in front of audiences. The Alumni Home Run Derby was an important first major opportunity, but the center fielder has hinted there could be more performances to come.
In August 2026, the singer-songwriter Ed Sheeran visited T-Mobile Park, and Rodriguez also discussed his DJing interest with him.
Sheeran told Rodriguez to keep practicing and honing the skill, even if friends or others don’t immediately respond positively to the music. The advice was a simple fact of learning a creative discipline: to improve, you have to repeat and persevere.
What Rodriguez has in store for DJ Pleno is still up in the air. He’s said he’d like to do some original music and play for bigger crowds, but has also teased another possible project during the offseason.
The point of this story is that this DJ persona was purposefully created away from baseball. Rodriguez has long been known as a star for the Seattle Mariners, but 'DJ Pleno' gives him a space to be creative on his own.
For now, 'DJ Pleno' is a budding identity, not a substitute for Julio Rodriguez’s baseball career, but an addition to it. The Seattle Mariners star is creating a name for himself on the pitch, and house music is providing him with another outlet for expression.

item.title: [macombdaily.com] Tigers had the perfect sendoff for Miguel Cabrera. Can they do it again for Justin Verlander?
item.dc:creator: Tribune News Service
item.description: By Evan Woodbery, mlive.com DETROIT — The Detroit Tigers were working off a loose script for how they hoped Miguel Cabrera’s final game would end in 2023. item.content:encoded:
By Evan Woodbery, mlive.com
DETROIT — The Detroit Tigers were working off a loose script for how they hoped Miguel Cabrera’s final game would end in 2023.
Some of the best parts, however, weren’t in the script.
Cabrera had struck out twice and popped out in his first three plate appearances against the Cleveland Guardians on the final day of the season. When he walked in the seventh inning, hardly the storybook ending anyone had envisioned, umpires asked Tigers manager A.J. Hinch if he wanted to stop the game.
Hinch told them to keep playing.
He still had one more scene in mind.
Cabrera, who had not played the field since 2021 and no longer even owned a glove, borrowed one from Spencer Torkelson and trotted to first base for the top of the eighth. His teammates intentionally stayed behind in the dugout for a few moments, leaving Cabrera alone on the field to soak in the cheers.
Then baseball provided the part nobody could have planned.
Steven Kwan hit the first ball of the inning directly to Cabrera, who fielded it and raced to first base for the out. Hinch emerged from the dugout with Cabrera’s three children and removed him from a major-league game for the final time.
It was, as Hinch recalled Tuesday, “the most perfect sendoff of all time.”
Three years later, Hinch is trying to help another Tigers icon reach the finish line.
Justin Verlander will make the final start of his 21-season career on Saturday against the Pittsburgh Pirates at Comerica Park. Once again, the Tigers would love to send one of the greatest players in franchise history into retirement with just the right final moment.
There’s just one problem.
Starting pitchers are a lot harder to script.
“I felt like we could create the moment for [Cabrera] regardless of performance,” Hinch said. “Pitching’s a little bit different.”
With Cabrera, the Tigers controlled much of the setup, except, of course, for Kwan hitting the grounder to first. That was pure baseball serendipity.
With Verlander, almost everything that happens after the first pitch will depend on Verlander himself, the Pirates and the unpredictable rhythm of a baseball game.
Surely the easiest script would be to put Verlander on the mound, wait for something good to happen, perhaps a strikeout, then have Hinch walk out from the dugout and allow Verlander to leave to a standing ovation.
But Verlander has already made clear that he doesn’t want that.
“I don’t just want to go out there and do the one inning and come out and wave,” Verlander said Tuesday. “I would like to toe the rubber one more time in a competitive way and try to win the Detroit Tigers a ballgame.”
Exactly how long that means is anyone’s guess, including Verlander’s.
“No idea. No idea,” he said when asked about his limits.
He told Hinch he would communicate honestly about how he feels Saturday.
“If things are going well and I’m out there and having some success, it doesn’t need to be a perfect game for me to be able to stay out there,” Verlander said. “If I’m able to continue to be healthy and I feel good, who knows what’s going to happen?”
Hinch joked that the ideal scenario would be simple enough.
“We would love the nine-inning no-hitter sendoff,” he said.
Nobody is expecting that, especially from a 43-year-old pitcher who has spent most of the year rehabbing.
The Tigers don’t need Verlander to be perfect Saturday. They don’t even need him to pitch particularly deep into the game.
But they would, naturally, prefer to find the right moment to end it.
A strikeout to finish an inning? Easy enough.
A clean inning after a couple of early jams? That works, too.
But what if Verlander feels good and wants another inning? What if the first batter of that inning doubles? What if the Pirates string together hits? At what point does Hinch decide the competitive portion of Verlander’s afternoon is over and the farewell can begin?
Unlike Cabrera’s final game, there is no defensive position to send him to and no guarantee that baseball will provide an obvious opening.
“The unknown right now is how Justin is going to respond physically to the challenge on Saturday with hitters in the box,” Hinch said. “And there’s no concession on the other side. They’re not just going to get out and make it nice and easy for him.”
That’s important to Verlander.
He wants Saturday to be a farewell, but he also wants it to be baseball.
“He wants to win the game and he wants to contribute to a win and he wants to do his part,” Hinch said.
And somewhere within that competition, Hinch hopes to find the right moment for the sendoff, whether it follows the script or not.
“I do appreciate trying to build the moment to the right time where we can properly say thank you,” he said.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Pete Alonso unanimously named Most Valuable Oriole
item.dc:creator: Mark Brown
item.description: For a lot of the season, there has seemed to be only one obvious choice to end up as the Most Valuable Oriole. You never know if some voters will talk themselves into something silly to stop it from being unanimous. In 2026, it was so obvious that even those people got it right. Pete Alonso was announced ahead of Wednesday's doubleheader as the Most Valuable Oriole for this season. The only real downer about Alonso's first season as an Oriole is the fact that so much of the roster around him was
item.content:encoded:
For a lot of the season, there has seemed to be only one obvious choice to end up as the Most Valuable Oriole. You never know if some voters will talk themselves into something silly to stop it from being unanimous. In 2026, it was so obvious that even those people got it right. Pete Alonso was announced ahead of Wednesday's doubleheader as the Most Valuable Oriole for this season.
The only real downer about Alonso's first season as an Oriole is the fact that so much of the roster around him was incapable for large stretches of the season of doing its part to make this a good Orioles team. Alonso's 40 homers, .265/.359/.510 batting line, and 4.6 bWAR (hopefully with more to come over the last five games) were, in some sense, "wasted." The team will probably be eliminated from postseason contention officially today.
That doesn't take entirely away from the joy that Alonso has brought to the Orioles. He's also brought better-than-advertised first base defense. If he doesn't win a Gold Glove, that would be an egregious snub. He seems excited to be an Oriole in a way that comes along maybe once or twice in a decade, and his sign-off of every interview with "Let's go O's" is charming. We can all feel good about that contract going for four more years, at least for now.
The unanimous selection of Alonso marked the first time that the team had a unanimous winner since Cedric Mullins was the choice in 2021. That was the year that Mullins had the 30 home run/30 stolen base season for the Orioles, breaking out at the plate after giving up on being a switch hitter.
The Orioles do not announce the exact vote breakdown, or even who votes for this award. It is a mystery list of media and broadcasters who cover the team. Camden Chat is not included on that list. Ballots are submitted with a first place, second place, and third place, and the winner is tallied based on a points system. It's easy when it's unanimous for first place.
What the Orioles do announce is a list of players who did not win but also received votes. These guys were all on at least one voter's ballot, in addition to the unanimous winner, Alonso: Blaze Alexander, Samuel Basallo, Shane Baz, Kyle Bradish, Christian Encarnacion-Strand, Rico Garcia, Gunnar Henderson, Trevor Rogers, and Brandon Young.
Weird votes are typically a fixture of this opaque process. Last year was a bigger "weird vote" year – somebody actually voted for interim manager Tony Mansolino a year ago. Somebody else, or maybe the same person, voted for Dylan Carlson, who was a -0.7 bWAR player for the 2025 Orioles. Most of these guys on the 2026 list were at least good for part of the season and can be somewhat justified as choices. Nobody voted for Craig Albernaz or this year's negative bWAR outfielders, Dylan Beavers and Leody Taveras.
In the case of Alexander and Encarnacion-Strand, they just didn't get to play enough to demonstrate more value; their overall performance was good in the games that they played. Alexander missed a bunch of games due to getting bones broken by a hit by pitch. Encarnacion-Strand only arrived in the organization during the season. He might turn out to be a Ryan O'Hearn kind of late bloomer story, or he might turn out to be a Jeremiah Jackson kind of flash in the plan.
When it comes to guys like Bradish, Henderson, Rogers, and Mayo, they weren't good for significant portions of the season, so their season numbers don't look like anything special. You have to squint more for some than for others to see the case. Mayo is closing out the season with three excellent months. Henderson has been hitting well since about mid-August and has maintained value with solid shortstop defense – that's not to say it's flawless, but the good has outweighed the bad even in what is another disappointing year for him overall. For Bradish, I don't know. It felt good when he got that contract extension.
For me, Alonso is at the top, followed by Young and Rogers. Young's surprisingly-good season was probably the only thing that prevented the Orioles from being completely buried in May or June. The team is 19-8 in Young starts this year. Whoever voted for Baz clearly didn't hold the team's 10-21 record in his starts against him. Baz probably "deserves" like 15-16 in his starts.
After Alonso and Young, you can make the case for a lot of people as third place, and that's reflected in the variety of names who also received votes. Rogers was not good in April and May but has looked like a fringe Cy Young candidate ever since. That picks up on last year, when he was a Cy Young-caliber pitcher in the 18 starts that he made. That's why I'd pick him for the third place spot; Rogers was the MVO winner a year ago.
Somebody's going to pay Rogers this offseason. I don't have any hope that it will be the Orioles.

item.title: [MLB.com] Alonso named unanimous winner of '26 Most Valuable Oriole Award
item.dc:creator: Jake Rill
item.description: BALTIMORE -- Every season, one Baltimore player receives the Most Valuable Oriole Award, an honor that is voted on by members of the local print and broadcast media who cover the team on a regular basis. And some years, it can be a difficult decision resulting in a close race. That was not the case in 2026. Pete Alonso was unanimously named the winner of this year’s Most Valuable Oriole Award, the club announced Wednesday. The 31-year-old slugger was the runaway favorite for the recognition, as
item.content:encoded:
BALTIMORE -- Every season, one Baltimore player receives the Most Valuable Oriole Award, an honor that is voted on by members of the local print and broadcast media who cover the team on a regular basis. And some years, it can be a difficult decision resulting in a close race.
That was not the case in 2026.
Pete Alonso was unanimously named the winner of this year’s Most Valuable Oriole Award, the club announced Wednesday. The 31-year-old slugger was the runaway favorite for the recognition, as he was clearly the team’s top player during his first season in Baltimore.
Ballots included up to three players, with points tabulated in a 5-3-1 format (for first, second and third, respectively). The other O’s players to receive votes this year were utility man Blaze Alexander, catcher Samuel Basallo, right-hander Shane Baz, right-hander Kyle Bradish, infielder Christian Encarnacion-Strand, right-hander Rico Garcia, shortstop Gunnar Henderson, infielder Coby Mayo, left-hander Trevor Rogers and right-hander Brandon Young.
But nobody was coming close to Alonso, who has lived up to lofty expectations since signing a five-year, $155 million deal to join the Orioles last December.
Alonso has been racking up honors of late, as he was the Orioles’ nominee for the Roberto Clemente Award and also their recipient of the Heart & Hustle Award. Now, he’s the Most Valuable Oriole -- the first unanimous winner since outfielder Cedric Mullins in 2021 -- and it wouldn’t be surprising if he finishes quite high in American League MVP Award voting after his strong conclusion to the season.
Entering Wednesday, Alonso led Baltimore in hits (156), runs scored (94), home runs (40), RBIs (108), batting average (.265), slugging percentage (.510) and OPS (.869). He’s also the only O’s player to start all 157 games this season.
All of the numbers are impressive. But Alonso’s power and run production have stood out most.
Now sitting at 304 career home runs, Alonso has clubbed at least 37 homers in six of his eight MLB seasons and has reached the 40-homer mark four times. The Polar Bear is the ninth player in Orioles history (since 1954) to hit 40 in a season, marking the 10th overall occurrence.
Alonso’s 108 RBIs are the most in the AL. He is on pace to become the first player in AL/NL history to post a season in which he led the league in RBIs in both leagues. (Alonso had a National League-high 131 RBIs for the Mets in 2022.)
The stats have never been the most important thing to Alonso, though.
“I just want to leave it all out there,” Alonso recently said. “I really love playing the game, and for me, I just want to be all I can be and do whatever I can every single night to win the game, you know? I really take pride in wanting to win and giving it all I have.”
The Orioles (76-81 entering Wednesday) are unlikely to reach the postseason, as they’re close to elimination. But Alonso has four more years remaining on his contract and is hopeful he can lead the club back to the playoffs as soon as possible.
Players to win MVO in first season with Orioles
OF Chuck Diering (1954)
OF Dave Philley (1955)
RHP Stu Miller (1963)
OF Frank Robinson (1966)
OF Ken Singleton (1975)
RHP Rodrigo Lopez (2002, rookie)
SS Miguel Tejada (2004)
DH Nelson Cruz (2014)
C Adley Rutschman (2022, rookie)
1B Pete Alonso (2026)
Alonso has hit well, played strong defense at first base and become a leader inside Baltimore’s clubhouse. He’s been an even better fit with the O’s than those in the organization could have imagined he’d be this past winter.
“My belief on any long-term contract is, if you’re going to do anything over three years -- especially when you get into the five-year, 10-year range -- that person has to have behaviors that impact the environment. You want that guy to have a compound effect where he gets people better,” bench coach Donnie Ecker said. “Pete’s up there with the best I’ve seen, just in terms of caring for the people around him and really not ever settling for average.”

item.title: [Empire Sports Media] Cody Bellinger saved the Yankees' afternoon but the bigger problem survived
item.dc:creator: Alexander Wilson
item.description: Cody Bellinger hit the ball out in the fourth inning, and for a few hours the Yankees had exactly what they needed. His two-run shot was the entire offense in a 2-0 win over Tampa Bay. Carlos Rodon gave them eight scoreless innings. No one needed to discuss the lineup after that first game. The second game changed the conversation. New York lost 6-1, scored only three runs across the doubleheader and watched the Rays clinch the division. item.content:encoded:
Cody Bellinger hit the ball out in the fourth inning, and for a few hours the Yankees had exactly what they needed. His two-run shot was the entire offense in a 2-0 win over Tampa Bay. Carlos Rodon gave them eight scoreless innings. No one needed to discuss the lineup after that first game.
The second game changed the conversation. New York lost 6-1, scored only three runs across the doubleheader and watched the Rays clinch the division. Bellinger’s swing won a game; it did not make the Yankees’ scoring issue disappear.
The Yankees needed that homer from Bellinger
There is a difference between calling one swing a cure and appreciating what it did. Bellinger has 17 home runs and 73 RBI with a .268 average and .779 OPS after Tuesday. He does not need to hit 40 homers to help this club, but his power has to show up in the games where one mistake pitch can decide the result.
He got that pitch from Nick Martinez and did not miss it. The sight of Bellinger rounding the bases mattered more because the Yankees were playing without much margin for error. It was also a reminder that Ben Rice and the rest of the order cannot leave the run production to one man every afternoon.
Tuesday’s opener was a clean illustration of how this team wins when the bats are light: a dominant starter, one big hit and a quiet ninth inning. The evening loss was the other side of the same bet.
A good afternoon cannot carry the whole Yankees lineup
I liked the homer, especially against the club New York spent months chasing. I do not think it is fair to treat it as proof the offense is ready for three October games in a row. Drew Rasmussen held the Yankees down in the nightcap, and they did not find another answer until it was too late.
With Aaron Judge’s availability already under a microscope, the supporting bats have to contribute more than an occasional solo moment. Bellinger delivered on Tuesday. The Yankees still need several hitters to do the same when a short series starts.

item.content:encoded:
The Orioles today announced that first baseman PETE ALONSO has been unanimously voted the winner of the 2026 Louis M. Hatter Most Valuable Oriole Award by members of the local media who cover the team on a regular basis. He will be recognized for his accomplishments during an on-field ceremony prior to tonight’s game against the Toronto Blue Jays.
Alonso is the eighth first baseman (18th instance) in franchise history to be named Most Valuable Oriole, joining JIM GENTILE (1961), BOOG POWELL (1969-1970), LEE MAY (1976), EDDIE MURRAY (1978, 1981-1985, and 1988), RAFAEL PALMEIRO (1995-1996 and 1998), JEFF CONINE (2001), and CHRIS DAVIS (2013 and 2015). He is also the first to be named the unanimous winner of the award since CEDRIC MULLINS in 2021.
The right-handed slugger is slashing .265/.359/.510 (156-for-588) with 24 doubles, 40 home runs, 94 runs, 108 RBI, 78 walks (5 IBB), 11 hit-by-pitches, and five stolen bases, starting all 157 games for the Orioles this season. He enters play today leading the American League in RBI while ranking third in homers, third in total bases (300), fifth in slugging percentage, fifth in OPS (.869), sixth in extra-base hits (64), seventh in hits, and eighth in runs. He paces all Orioles hitters in hits, homers, runs, RBI, total bases, and extra-base hits. Alonso has played in 573 consecutive games, the second-longest active streak in the majors behind Atlanta’s Matt Olson (939 G).
The 31-year-old leads the Orioles with 4.6 Baseball Reference Wins Above Replacement (bWAR) and 4.5 Fangraphs Wins Above Replacement (fWAR), ranking first among all MLB first basemen in fWAR. His 4.6 bWAR is the highest by an Orioles first baseman since CHRIS DAVIS (4.9 bWAR) in 2015.
Alonso earned AL Player of the Week honors for the week of August 10-16 when he slashed .545/.630/.864 (12-for-22) with one double, two home runs, five runs, five RBI, and four walks in six games played. He was the first Oriole to earn the honor since GUNNAR HENDERSON on September 7, 2024, and the first Orioles first baseman since RYAN MOUNTCASTLE on June 5, 2021.
This season, he became the eighth Oriole to hit at least 30 home runs in his first season with the team, joining FRANK ROBINSON (49 in 1966), MARK TRUMBO (47 in 2016), NELSON CRUZ (40 in 2014), MARK REYNOLDS (37 in 2011), ALBERT BELLE (37 in 1999), MIGUEL TEJADA (34 in 2004), and J.J. HARDY (30 in 2011). He also became the fifth player in MLB history to hit 30+ home runs in at least seven of his first eight seasons, joining Mark Teixeira, Albert Pujols, Eddie Mathews, and Ralph Kiner. On September 21, he became the ninth Oriole (10th occurrence) with a 40-homer season, joining CHRIS DAVIS (53 in 2013 and 47 in 2015), BRADY ANDERSON (50 in 1996), FRANK ROBINSON (49 in 1966), MARK TRUMBO (47 in 2016), JIM GENTILE (46 in 1961), ANTHONY SANTANDER (44 in 2024), RAFAEL PALMEIRO(43 in 1998), and NELSON CRUZ (40 in 2014).
The Most Valuable Oriole Award is named in honor of the late LOU HATTER, a former sportswriter for The Baltimore Sun who covered the Orioles for 27 years. Balloting for the Most Valuable Oriole Award concluded last week, with voting on a 5-3-1 basis. Ten other players received a second or third-place vote: BLAZE ALEXANDER, SAMUEL BASALLO, SHANE BAZ, KYLE BRADISH, CHRISTIAN ENCARNACION-STRAND, RICO GARCIA, GUNNAR HENDERSON, COBY MAYO, TREVOR ROGERS, and BRANDON YOUNG.
