item.content:encoded:
Ronald Acuña Jr. suma su tercera temporada con al menos 20 jonrones y 20 bases robadas en MLB y entra al top 3 entre venezolanos.
Ronald Acuña Jr. sigue escribiendo su nombre en la historia del béisbol venezolano. El outfielder de los Bravos de Atlanta cerró otra temporada con al menos 20 jonrones y 20 bases robadas, un logro que pocos han repetido con tanta consistencia. Acuña alcanza su tercera campaña 20-20 y con eso se suma a un grupo selecto de compatriotas que marcaron época en Grandes Ligas.
El camino no fue sencillo. Las lesiones interrumpieron su ritmo en varios momentos y limitaron su presencia en la alineación. Aun así, el criollo encontró la forma de producir cuando estuvo disponible y dejó números que respaldan su calidad. Su combinación de poder y velocidad lo mantiene como una pieza clave en el ataque de Atlanta y como referencia obligada al hablar de los mejores peloteros de Venezuela.
Este hito llega en un año en el que muchos dudaban de su capacidad para mantener el nivel de años anteriores y en el que las lesiones volvieron a estar presentes. Pese a esto los números de Acuña confirman su recuperación, algo que resulta clave tomando en cuenta que nos acercamos a octubre y que Atlanta lo necesita sano para poder pelear en playoffs.
MÁS INFORMACIÓN: Ronald Acuña Jr.: velocidad, poder y una nueva página en MLB
Qué significa la temporada 20-20 de Ronald Acuña Jr. en 2026
Una campaña 20-20 exige un buen desempeño en dos facetas claves de la ofensiva: pegarle fuerte a la bola y saber correr las bases con inteligencia. Acuña cumplió con ese doble requisito en 2026 y con eso llegó a su tercera temporada 20-20 en la MLB. Sus otras dos veces con al menos 20 jonrones y 20 bases robadas llegaron en 2019 y 2023, años en los que también dejó un perfil ofensivo completo, con poder en el bate y presión en las bases.
Acuña acumula 103 partidos en 2026, con 454 apariciones en el plato, 102 hits, 55 carreras impulsadas y 60 anotadas. Esos números reflejan un rendimiento sólido para un jugador que pasó por dos distensiones en el corva izquierda y que en varios tramos de la temporada no estuvo al 100%. Aun con esos obstáculos, el criollo fue capaz de dejar muy buenos números en esta temporada regular.
Este tipo de registro no depende solo de fuerza. También exige una excelente lectura de lanzamientos, disciplina en el plato y timing para robar algo que lo ha caracterizado a lo largo de su carrera. Hay que recordar que Acuña suma 225 bases robadas de por vida y 206 jonrones en su carrera regular, cifras que lo ubican en un nivel distinto dentro de la ofensiva venezolana en la MLB.
El club selecto de venezolanos con temporadas 20-20 en MLB
Pocos peloteros de Venezuela han logrado una campaña 20-20. El grupo lo encabezan Bobby Abreu, Carlos González y José Altuve, tres nombres que definieron épocas distintas y que dejaron huella en sus respectivas franquicias. Acuña se une a ese trío y con su tercera vez se ubica en el top 3 histórico de jonroneros venezolanos en Grandes Ligas, un escalón que pocos alcanzan y que mide impacto real en el juego.
Bobby Abreu marcó el estándar con la marca 20-20 en 9 temporadas a lo largo de su carrera en MLB, un número que refleja su combinación de poder y velocidad durante más de una década. Carlos González alcanzó ese registro en 4 ocasiones durante sus 12 campañas en la liga mayor, con picos de producción que lo llevaron a la élite del bateo. José Altuve, por su parte, suma 3 temporadas 20-20 con los Astros de Houston, un logro que respalda su perfil de bateador de contacto con velocidad en las bases.
La marca de Acuña también tiene un componente de resistencia. Llegar tres veces a 20-20 implica mantener salud relativa y rendimiento en distintos momentos de la carrera. El criollo ya tiene un MVP en 2023, un Rookie del Año en 2018 y un récord histórico de 40-70 en esa misma campaña del MVP. Esos logros, sumados a su tercera temporada 20-20, lo convierten en referencia para la nueva generación de peloteros venezolanos.
Lista completa de venezolanos con temporadas 20-20 en MLB
- Bob Abreu (9)
- Carlos González (4)
- Ronald Acuña Jr. (3)
- Jackson Chourio (3)
- José Altuve (3)
- Magglio Ordóñez (1)
- Elvis Andrus (1)
MÁS INFORMACIÓN: Ronald Acuña Jr. de regreso: el venezolano de los Braves que quiere recuperar su MVP tras superar la lesión de rodilla
Por qué Ronald Acuña Jr. sigue siendo clave para los Bravos y para Venezuela
Atlanta construye su ataque alrededor de la versatilidad. Acuña ofrece poder desde la parte alta del orden al bate, capacidad para estirar hits y presión constante sobre la defensa rival. Esa combinación hace que su presencia en el lineup, incluso con minutos limitados debido a las lesiones, cambie la dinámica del juego.
Acuña apenas tiene 28 años y ya suma tres campañas 20-20, una cifra que deja espacio para seguir creciendo. Su historial de poder y velocidad, sumado a su capacidad de ajuste, lo pone en ruta para añadir más temporadas con al menos 20 jonrones y 20 bases robadas. La gran incógnita ahora es si podrá igualar o superar las 9 veces de Bobby Abreu, el récord entre venezolanos en MLB. El tiempo dirá si el criollo se acerca a esa marca o si incluso la deja atrás.

item.title: [fansided.com] Dave Roberts' handling of Roki Sasaki shows why the Dodgers keep winning
item.dc:creator: Jake Elman
item.description: If you needed yet another reminder of why Dave Roberts has led the Los Angeles Dodgers to three championships in six years, look no further than his treatment of Roki Sasaki. Roberts has both built Sasaki up and held the Japanese import accountable through two up-and-down seasons. He hasn’t been stubbornly loyal to the 24-year-old righty, nor has he waved the white flag amid Sasaki’s continued control issues. As Sasaki nears a return from the IL, Roberts confirmed that Sasaki will start pitching
item.content:encoded:
If you needed yet another reminder of why Dave Roberts has led the Los Angeles Dodgers to three championships in six years, look no further than his treatment of Roki Sasaki.
Roberts has both built Sasaki up and held the Japanese import accountable through two up-and-down seasons. He hasn’t been stubbornly loyal to the 24-year-old righty, nor has he waved the white flag amid Sasaki’s continued control issues.
As Sasaki nears a return from the IL, Roberts confirmed that Sasaki will start pitching out of the bullpen this week. All signs point to Sasaki serving as a reliever for the second straight postseason.
Sasaki has missed nearly all of September with a hip injury, and he should have some extra time to recover. The Dodgers are closing in one of the NL’s top two playoff seeds, which includes a first-round bye.
Does Roki Sasaki deserve to make the Los Angeles Dodgers’ playoff roster?
Before looking ahead to October, let’s quickly travel back to this past spring. I repeatedly questioned Sasaki’s viability as an MLB starter, largely because of his control and what felt like an inability to handle the pressure associated with pitching Stateside.
Honestly? I really haven’t changed my opinion, though I’ll give Sasaki his flowers. He’s played some of his best baseball in the second half, recording a 3.05 ERA in seven starts. That’s down from 5.33 over 15 first-half outings, though he’s still struggling to make it through five innings.
Most importantly, he’s significantly cut down on his homers, allowing three in 38.1 innings. That’s a fantastic improvement from the 19 long balls he gave up in 81 first-half innings.
So what’s the problem? Walks. I’m old school, so I don’t like young pitchers only working five innings because they can’t hit the strike zone. Sasaki has issued 15 free passes in those 38.1 innings, and it drives up his pitch count.
At the end of the day, Sasaki has completed six innings in just seven of his 22 starts. Now is the perfect time to permanently transition him to a relief role.
But we asked whether Sasaki deserves to be on the playoff roster, and despite my criticism, the answer is an easy “yes.” There’s something to be said about a young player admitting to confidence issues yet powering through and trying to make things work rather than let things spiral.
What’s especially admirable about Sasaki is that he doesn’t complain or make himself out to be a victim. He’s never targeted the media, which has actually had his back for much of the last two years. He’s certainly not teammate Kyle Tucker, whose body language and work ethic have raised red flags dating back to his brief stint with the Cubs.
Maybe Sasaki is the Dodgers’ secret playoff weapon once again. We’d certainly feel more comfortable trusting him in October instead of embattled former closer Edwin Díaz.
Yikes. Imagine reading that on Opening Day.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Paul Skenes gets called out for World Baseball Classic excuse
item.dc:creator: Matt Larter
item.description: MLB fans and analysts aren't buying Pittsburgh Pirates ace Paul Skenes' explanation for his rocky 2026 season, after the star pitcher pointed to his World Baseball Classic appearance as the root cause of his struggles. Skenes claimed that pitching for Team USA at the WBC sapped his velocity and set off his decline this season, calling it the "root" of his issues. But critics were quick to point out that his statistics tell a different story. Skenes' excuse doesn't match the numbers Mar 3, 2026;
item.content:encoded:
MLB fans and analysts aren't buying Pittsburgh Pirates ace Paul Skenes' explanation for his rocky 2026 season, after the star pitcher pointed to his World Baseball Classic appearance as the root cause of his struggles.
Skenes claimed that pitching for Team USA at the WBC sapped his velocity and set off his decline this season, calling it the "root" of his issues. But critics were quick to point out that his statistics tell a different story.
Skenes' excuse doesn't match the numbers
Mar 3, 2026; Scottsdale, AZ, USA; Team USA pitcher Paul Skenes against the San Francisco Giants during a spring training game at Scottsdale Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Mark J. Rebilas-Imagn Images
Through his first nine starts of 2026, Skenes posted a 1.98 ERA — nearly identical to his starts at the same point in 2025 (1.97 ERA) and 2024 (1.96 ERA). His performance didn't actually dip until mid-May, well after his WBC appearances were behind him.
Since that mid-May turning point, Skenes has posted an ERA of 4.73, a steep decline that has pushed his overall mark for the season to a career-worst 3.91, along with a 1.13 WHIP through 31 games. The reigning National League Cy Young Award winner appeared twice for Team USA at the WBC, striking out seven over four scoreless innings against Mexico in round robin play and throwing 4.1 innings in a 2-1 semifinal win over the Dominican Republic.
Pirates season winds down out of contention
Aug 9, 2026; Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, USA; Pittsburgh Pirates pitcher Paul Skenes (30) walks out to the bullpen before the game against the New York Mets at PNC Park. Mandatory Credit: Charles LeClaire-Imagn Images
Skenes' individual struggles have played out against the backdrop of a disappointing Pirates campaign. Pittsburgh sits at 79-77 with just six games remaining, firmly out of playoff contention. The team is third in the National League Central, a massive 19 games behind the division-leading Milwaukee Brewers (98-58), and seven games back of the Philadelphia Phillies (86-70) for the final NL Wild Card spot.
The Pirates begin the penultimate series of their season on Tuesday, hosting the St. Louis Cardinals as they look to close out a forgettable year on a better note.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Fantasy Baseball League Winners: Pete Crow-Armstrong, Jordan Walker among players who helped managers the most in 2026
item.dc:creator: Fred Zinkie
item.description: In a player pool that is full of contributors, we are all looking for league winners — the players who outperform expectations to such a large degree that they carry teams to fantasy baseball championships. Here are the players who best fit the league winner label this season. And we have data to back it up, as these players have the highest roster rate among the top-500 teams across this vast platform. Let's look at where they came from, what they accomplished, and how successful they will be n
item.content:encoded:
In a player pool that is full of contributors, we are all looking for league winners — the players who outperform expectations to such a large degree that they carry teams to fantasy baseball championships.
Here are the players who best fit the league winner label this season. And we have data to back it up, as these players have the highest roster rate among the top-500 teams across this vast platform. Let's look at where they came from, what they accomplished, and how successful they will be next year. As you'll see, although we look for league winners on draft day, the best values are found on the waiver wire. After all, only two of the 10 players in this article (Sal Stewart, Pete Crow-Armstrong) were selected in more than 10% of Yahoo drafts.
Jordan Walker, OF, Cardinals: In head-to-head formats, Walker is far and away the leading roster member on top-500 teams, which is hardly surprising for someone who went from 6% drafted to sitting ninth overall on the Yahoo Player Rater. The 24-year-old still strikes out more often than the average hitter (25.9%), but his 100th-percentile bat speed has enabled him to rank among the top 15% of players in average exit velocity, barrel rate and hard-hit rate. Walker has also flashed his 92nd-percentile sprint speed by swiping 20 bases. There is room for a further uptick in steals and his power skills are sustainable, but there could be a slight pullback on his batting average. Overall, Walker belongs in the second round of 2027 drafts.
Bryan Baker, RP, Rays: The entire Rays bullpen was an afterthought in draft season. After all, the team was coming off a 77-win season, they lacked an established closer and the organization hadn't produced a 30-save pitcher since 2017. And those who drafted a Tampa reliever grabbed Griffin Jax or Edwin Uceta ahead of Baker. But Baker pitched the ninth inning of a four-run win on the second day of the season, picked up his first save of the campaign a week later and never looked back. I expect Baker to have some regression next season, as his 62:21 K:BB ratio is a good-not-great mark for an elite closer. But he will be a fine option once 5-6 relievers have come off the board.
Sal Stewart, 1B/2B/3B, Reds: Stewart gave us a preview of his potential late last season when he went deep five times in 18 games. But his exciting debut was only good enough to get him an ADP of 193.7 during draft season. Those who gave him a late-round opportunity quickly found out that they had struck gold, as the rookie had accumulated nine homers, 29 RBI and seven steals by the end of April. Stewart keeps his strikeout rate in check and regularly barrels up the baseball, which makes his 30-homer power sustainable. And anyone who looked at his minor league stats knew that he could swipe 15 bases. Like Walker, Stewart belongs in the second round of 2027 drafts.
Louis Varland, RP, Blue Jays: The season was nearly four weeks old when Varland earned his first save, but he made up for lost time and now ranks tied for fifth in the majors with 34 saves. The right-hander was a workhorse in high-leverage innings during the Blue Jays 2025 run to the World Series, which made him an obvious candidate to take over the ninth inning when Jeff Hoffman faltered for a second straight season. Varland strikes out batters in bunches and induces oodles of grounders, which should be a sustainable recipe for success. He's a top-five closer for 2027.
Parker Messick, SP, Guardians: This paragraph hurts to write, as I started the season by labelling Messick as my FOMO player of 2026. Although I loved his skills, I didn't draft the 25-year-old in many leagues, as I guessed that the Guardians would send him to Triple-A. I was wrong. Messick tossed six shutout innings on March 30 and never looked back. The southpaw ranks among the top 10 in baseball in ERA and WHIP, and his success is supported by a top-10 mark in xERA (3.09). Most managers will value Messick as a No. 2 starter in 2027, but I will likely value him as a low-end ace.
Logan Henderson, SP, Brewers: Although a back injury has kept Henderson under 20 starts, he has been spectacular when in the rotation. In fact, his 0.81 WHIP would rank second among qualified pitchers if he had enough innings to qualify. I expect some regression for Henderson, who is unlikely to enjoy a .219 BABIP for a second straight season. But I stopped doubting Milwaukee pitchers a long time ago, which means that I'll be happy to make the right-hander my No. 2 starter.
Jake McCarthy, OF, Rockies: McCarthy and Coors Field were a match made in heaven. The sparkplug limits strikeouts, so it makes sense that he would find success in the park that best boosts batting averages. Sure enough, McCarthy is hitting .318 with a .906 OPS at home, while maintaining average numbers (.275 BA, .747 OPS) on the road. McCarthy had already enjoyed a trio of 20-steal seasons as a part-time player in Arizona, so it's not surprising to see him reach the 30-steal plateau this year. McCarthy will be back with Colorado next year, so we can expect more of the same.
Pete Crow-Armstrong, OF, Cubs: Crow-Armstrong is the only player in this article who was a coveted commodity in March, as he was a fourth-round selection in most Yahoo drafts. By next March, the 24-year-old will be selected first overall in nearly every draft on the heels of what will likely be a 40-40 season. Nearly everything has improved for PCA this year, including his walk rate, strikeout rate and quality of contact. He could experience some regression and still sit atop the fantasy landscape.
Miguel Vargas, 1B/3B, White Sox: The massive breakout by Vargas has been somewhat understated in fantasy circles, for all the right reasons. The slugger hasn't enjoyed an attention-grabbing stretch but has instead been incredibly consistent from month-to-month. And instead of dominating a single category, Vargas has made significant contributions in all four counting-stat areas while maintaining a reasonable batting average. The best news is that Vargas has slightly underperformed his expected stats in every area, which makes a repeat of 2026 seem likely.
Cade Cavalli, SP, Nationals: The fingerprints of the new front office in Washington are all over the organization. The minor league teams have exceeded expectations, and James Wood and CJ Abrams have reached new heights while anchoring a vastly improved lineup. Cavalli is the team's biggest success story on the mound. He got off to a solid start before really turning things on (8-1, 1.90 ERA, 90:16 K:BB ratio) in the second half. Cavalli hasn't been lucky, as his .307 BABIP and 76.6% strand rate are normal marks and the ERA estimators give him ratios that are similar to his actual mark. The one cause for concern is that Cavalli's Stuff+ (102) and Location+ (99) numbers are mediocre. He's a No. 2 starter for 2027, and I will likely rank him behind Messick and Henderson.

item.title: [heavy.com] Yankees Announce Paul Goldschmidt Decision Before Rays Doubleheader
item.dc:creator: Jonathan Vankin
item.description: The New York Yankees are coming off two straight losses in Arizona to the Diamondbacks, a setback that left them a full six games behind the Tampa Bay Rays in the American League East pennant race. item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees are coming off two straight losses in Arizona to the Diamondbacks, a setback that left them a full six games behind the Tampa Bay Rays in the American League East pennant race.
But the Yankees still have a chance to win the division and with it, the top seed in the AL and a bye out of the wild-card playoff round.
The Yankees and Rays open a four-game, head-to-head series with the first game of a doubleheader Tuesday at Yankee Stadium. With a four-game sweep, the Yankees would take the season series. They would then need to sweep the Baltimore Orioles while the Rays lose two of three to the Philadelphia Phillies, or win two of three from Baltimore while the Rays are swept, to finish tied or ahead.
Before Game 1 of the doubleheader, the Yankees announced a decision on how they will utilize veteran first baseman Paul Goldschmidt.
Goldschmidt is out of the New York Yankees lineup for a third consecutive start, out of the lineup again because of a stark platoon split against right-handed pitching.
The pattern has held all September, and it likely has fans wondering about how much longer the 39-year-old holds even a part-time role with October two weeks away.

|---|---|---|---|---|
| SP: Carlos Rodón (LHP) • 6-3, 2.95 ERA | | | | |
| September 22, 2026 • Yankee Stadium, Bronx, NY • 1:05 PM ET • Rays at Yankees | | | | |
| # | Player | Pos | AVG | SLG |
| 1 | Ben Rice | DH | .261 | .528 |
| 2 | Cody Bellinger | LF | .270 | .435 |
| 3 | Heliot Ramos | RF | .241 | .409 |
| 4 | Luis García Jr. | 1B | .281 | .532 |
| 5 | George Lombard Jr. | SS | .235 | .386 |
| 6 | Spencer Jones | CF | .248 | .442 |
| 7 | Anthony Volpe | 2B | .248 | .340 |

| 9 | José Caballero | 3B | .236 | .373 |
| Lineups confirmed. Season stats shown (AVG / SLG). Umpire: Sean Barber • Weather: 63°, Wind 13 mph • O/U: 7 Runs • Line: TB +112 / NYY -135. | | | | |
Boone’s Platoon Explains Goldschmidt Sit
Aaron Boone’s lineup card for Tuesday’s series opener against Tampa Bay leaves Goldschmidt out again, extending a run that traces back to Saturday. He started Friday against left-hander Eduardo Rodriguez in Arizona and went 1-for-4 with a walk and two runs, then sat both weekend games against right-handers Brandon Pfaadt and Corbin Burnes. That’s three benchings in the last three games against right-handed starters.
Why? Goldschmidt has produced an elite 1.006 OPS against lefties this season but an anemic .572 mark versus right-handers, a gap wide enough that Boone starts Ben Rice at DH and Luis García Jr. at first whenever a right-hander pitches. An The Athletic report on the lineup moves after Aaron Judge’s calf strain named Goldschmidt and Heliot Ramos as the bats Boone leans on against lefties, with García handling the right-handed side.
Nick Martinez, Tuesday’s Tampa Bay starter, has largely dominated Goldschmidt in his career. The former National League MVP is 2-for-10 with four walks and two strikeouts against Martinez, and he is 0-for-13 with four strikeouts in his last three meetings with the right-hander since 2024. Martinez enters at 15-4 with a 2.94 ERA this year, and beat the Yankees in the Bronx in May, giving Boone both the season splits and the head-to-head history pointing toward a Goldschmidt benching.
Tuesday’s day-night doubleheader against two more right-handed Rays starters gives Boone an easy excuse to sit the 39-year-old.
| TAMPA BAY RAYS STARTING LINEUP (GAME 1) | | | | |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| SP: Nick Martinez (RHP) • 15-4, 2.94 ERA | | | | |
| September 22, 2026 • Yankee Stadium, Bronx, NY • 1:05 PM ET • Rays at Yankees | | | | |
| # | Player | Pos | AVG | SLG |
| 1 | Yandy Díaz | DH | .292 | .807 |
| 2 | Jonathan Aranda | 1B | .277 | .800 |
| 3 | Junior Caminero | 3B | .277 | .892 |
| 4 | Liam Hicks | C | .288 | .811 |
| 5 | Chandler Simpson | LF | .309 | .697 |
| 6 | Jonny DeLuca | CF | .259 | .700 |
| 7 | Víctor Mesa Jr. | RF | .251 | .825 |
| 8 | Jorge Mateo | SS | .207 | .573 |
| 9 | Richie Palacios | 2B | .234 | .707 |
| Lineups confirmed. Season stats shown (AVG / OPS). Umpire: Sean Barber • Weather: 63°, Wind 13 mph • O/U: 7 Runs • Line: TB +112 / NYY -135. | | | | |
Goldschmidt’s Future in New York
Goldschmidt becomes a free agent again this winter, and the Yankees have made no public commitment either way. A cheap return as a lefty-masher and clubhouse mentor remains plausible given Rice’s grip on first base, and his credentials, a 2022 NL MVP award, seven All-Star selections, four Gold Gloves and five Silver Sluggers still make him a name teams will inquire about this winter.
First base belongs to Rice, who has grown into an everyday role with 39 home runs and 95 RBI this season, pushing Goldschmidt into a complementary, short-side platoon job. That role fits the final stretch of a one-year, $4 million contract that can grow by $500,000 at each of four plate-appearance thresholds, according to Spotrac, a modest deal compared with the $12.5 million he earned in his first Yankees season a year earlier.

item.title: [Líder en deportes] Vladimir Guerrero Jr. está día a día por molestias en la espalda
item.dc:creator: Jesús David Castellano
item.description: El primera base dominicano de los Azulejos de Toronto, Vladimir Guerrero Jr., quedó fuera de la alineación para el primero de la serie ante los Orioles de Baltimore —encuentro que terminó en derrota por pizarra de 4-3 el lunes en Camden Yards—, al experimentar tensión en la parte inferior de la espalda. Lee también: Eduardo Valencia deja buenas sensaciones en su primer año El infielder ha lidiado con molestias en la espalda durante toda la temporada, las cuales ha superado al punto de seguir act
item.content:encoded:
El primera base dominicano de los Azulejos de Toronto, Vladimir Guerrero Jr., quedó fuera de la alineación para el primero de la serie ante los Orioles de Baltimore —encuentro que terminó en derrota por pizarra de 4-3 el lunes en Camden Yards—, al experimentar tensión en la parte inferior de la espalda.
Lee también: Eduardo Valencia deja buenas sensaciones en su primer año
El infielder ha lidiado con molestias en la espalda durante toda la temporada, las cuales ha superado al punto de seguir activo; sin embargo, la dolencia se agravó hace varios días cuando se estiró para completar una jugada en la inicial. Además, el domingo escaló hasta afectar su swing lo suficiente como para que el equipo lo retirara del último de la serie ante los Rangers de Texas en la parte baja del cuarto episodio.
Tras la derrota en Baltimore, los Azulejos se alejaron a tres juegos y medio del tercer comodín de la Liga Americana, ocupado por los Medias Blancas de Chicago, equipo que de paso posee el desempate a su favor. Este panorama complica aún más las remotas esperanzas del conjunto canadiense de avanzar a la postemporada.
Se nota al hacer swing
Pese a la situación, el mánager de los Azulejos, John Schneider, espera que su pupilo regrese pronto a la alineación, independientemente del contexto de la lucha por un comodín. «Siempre y cuando se sienta mejor y no esté realmente incómodo al batear», dijo el timonel, quien añadió que el estatus del jugador «realmente es día a día».
En ese sentido, el estratega de 46 años explicó el origen de la molestia: «Ocurre más cuando está aterrizando y rotando. Podías verlo en algunos de sus swings ayer. Sabíamos desde el principio que estaba un poco tenso, pero no estaba realmente logrando su swing habitual».
Vladimir Guerrero Jr. podría tener algo de tiempo para recuperarse, sobre todo si los pronósticos de lluvia trastocan los juegos del martes y el miércoles, previo a la última serie de los Azulejos en casa ante los Rojos de Cincinnati.

item.content:encoded:
Why Ronald Acuna Jr.'s brother is one of the worst hitters in MLB for White Sox originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The Chicago White Sox lost 121 games just two seasons ago.
Now, they are fighting to make the postseason and win the division for the first time since 2021.
Chicago is one game behind the Cleveland Guardians for first place in the AL Central standings.
To book an automatic trip to the ALDS, the White Sox will need productive weeks from the everyday players.
However, it may also include their bench players, some of whom are having a better offensive year than others.
Outfielder and shortstop Luisangel Acuna, the younger brother of Atlanta Braves star outfielder Ronald Acuna Jr., is having a poor season at the plate.
In fact, Acuna's offensive performance has been one of the worst in the Majors. Bleacher Report's Zachary D. Rymer named him Chicago's worst player of 2026.
"To be fair, Edgar Quero has taken exactly as many plate appearances (217) as Acuña and has been even more of a straggler, to the tune of -0.8 rWAR. At least he's off the roster, whereas Acuña is still doing the bad kind of damage," Rymer wrote.
In 98 games, Acuna has a .227/.260/.261 slash line with just one home run and a .522 OPS.
"He has only a 47 OPS+ for the season, making him 53 percent worse than the average hitter. Among hitters with at least 200 plate appearances, only three have been less productive at the plate," Rymer added.
Acuna may not see much playing time in the postseason, but he can provide value with his legs.
The 24-year-old has 17 stolen bases in 23 attempts and ranks in the 98th percentile for sprint speed.

Well, in Year 1 of his new deal, he has shown no signs of slowing down. He is also hitting .265 this season. His 40th ho
item.content:encoded:
Pete Alonso has been everything the Baltimore Orioles could have hoped for since signing him to a five-year, $155 million deal in the offseason.
Alonso hit his 39th and 40th home runs in Monday night's win over the Toronto Blue Jays. Some teams were reportedly hesitant to pay Alonso in free agency because they were unsure if he could maintain his power numbers as he got older. Well, in Year 1 of his new deal, he has shown no signs of slowing down. He is also hitting .265 this season.
His 40th home run for the Orioles carries some historical significance. Alonso hit 53 home runs in his rookie year on the New York Mets in the National League. His 40th home run in his first year as part of an American League team makes him the only player in MLB history to hit at least 40 home runs in his first season in each league, according to OptaSTATS.
Since 2019, when Alonso made his debut, only Kyle Schwarber has hit more home runs than him. Schwarber is two years older than Alonso and may be a good example of how Alonso will age. Schwarber strikes out a ton and does not have a good batting average. However, he hits home runs at a very high clip and is currently tied for the most home runs in baseball.
Alonso and the Orioles may not make the postseason, but Alonso proved he deserved to be paid handsomely and should be a key player for the Orioles in the near future as they look to get back to playing baseball in October.
More MLB: What Will Cubs Do If Alex Bregman Is Not Ready For Wild Card Series?

item.content:encoded:
The Chicago Cubs have been fortunate to have the best player in Major League Baseball play for them this season, as Pete Crow-Armstrong is doing things not seen in a long time.
He's playing elite defense out in center field and is adding a lot of offense, with an MLB-leading 45 homers, to his season production as well. There is no denying PCA has been the best position player this year, and of the last few decades as well.
ESPN's Jeff Passan compared Crow-Armstrong to a prime Mike Trout, a future Hall of Famer who was playing at such a high level he was considered one of the greatest players of all time. This is some high praise for PCA, but its' deserved.
Pete Crow-Armstrong gets deserving comparison to prime Mike Trout
"Best Prime Mike Trout Impression: Pete Crow-Armstrong," Passan writes. "... One look at 10-win seasons by outfielders in the past half-century illustrates that. Only five players have reached that mark: Barry Bonds five times, Aaron Judge three, Mike Trout two, and Rickey Henderson, Mookie Betts and Crow-Armstrong one time apiece."
Going by fWAR, Crow-Armstrong is above 10 fWAR, joining some exclusive company. Of the outfielders to also accomplish this feat, Trout stands out as the most comparable player to PCA.
This season, with a few more games to go, Crow-Armstrong has hit 45 home runs with 107 RBIs and 118 runs scored, 30 doubles, eight triples, and 38 stolen bases. He's also put up elite defense in center field and has an NL-best .949 OPS and 157 OPS+.
He's a lock for the NL MVP this season, and while his bWAR total of 9.6 won't likely reach Trout's best bWAR seasons of 10.4 and 10.5, prime Trout is a worthy comparison.
Trout has had some incredible years in his career; four reached at least 9.5 bWAR. While a prime Trout had a higher OPS than PCA does this year, with Trout posting an OPS+ north of 157 for 11 straight seasons between 2012 and 2022.
While Trout might have the advantage in overall offensive production, Crow-Armstrong has been a better defender out in center field and has a more consistent base-stealing ability. Trout's peak season of 49 steals in 2012 is unreachable for PCA this year.
Crow-Armstrong has played at a similarly high level as Trout did during his prime, and this comparison from Passan is more than deserved for the Cubs superstar outfielder set to receive his first MVP award once the season comes to a close.

item.title: [heavy.com] Riley Greene, AJ Hinch Offer Blunt Message After Tigers' Elimination
item.dc:creator: Michael Whitaker
item.description: The Detroit Tigers entered the 2026 MLB campaign having qualified for the postseason two years in a row, and they had their eyes set on advancing further this time around. item.content:encoded:
The Detroit Tigers entered the 2026 MLB campaign having qualified for the postseason two years in a row, and they had their eyes set on advancing further this time around.
However, they ran into injury concerns along with a frustrating inability to hold on to late-game leads, and they were mathematically eliminated from any chance of a playoff berth with less than 10 games remaining in the campaign.
The season isn’t quite over yet, as they have five games remaining. However, there is a natural feeling of disappointment in the air.
Riley Greene, AJ Hinch Speak Bluntly After Detroit Tigers’ Elimination From Playoff Contention
Once their elimination from any chance of a playoff spot became official, skipper AJ Hinch and outfielder Riley Greene both offered blunt takes.
“Yeah, it sucks. We’ve been there the past two years, and our goal is to win the World Series, and we came up short,” Greene said on Monday to Brad Galli via X, formerly known as Twitter. “It’s been tough. Of course, there’s gonna be injuries and things are gonna happen, but at the end of the day, we didn’t win enough baseball games.”
Meanwhile, Hinch didn’t pull any punches – the club fell short of their goals they had in mind coming into this season.
“As we look back, despite all the ups and downs and roller coaster that this season went on, we fell seven days short,” he said. “There are things that we could have done better to alleviate things as a group. We talked about that.”
AJ Hinch Gathered His Players Together Following Their Elimination
Meanwhile, Hinch said that he gathered all players together to speak to them, saying that it’s a practice he’s maintained throughout his managerial career.
“Because it’s something that I’ve always done,” Hinch said via The Detroit News. “I want the day marked on the calendar when you’re mathematically eliminated.”
“I mean, the reality is that we’re eliminated, so we have to stare that right in the face and realize there’s seven days left where we don’t factor in,” he continued. “And we’re not playing playoff teams, either. So it’s a different environment. But once you get over the reality check, then you get to the responsibility of what the next six games need to be.”

item.title: [Pitcher List] Patience or Panic: Jackson Holliday, Mickey Moniak, Jung Hoo Lee
item.dc:creator: Josh Shaw

item.content:encoded:
Welcome to Week 25 of our Patience or Panic series! This is it. The end. If you’ve somehow clicked on this article and the title doesn’t make its premise clear, then I fear you may have to keep reading.
Jackson Holliday, 2B, Baltimore Orioles
Can’t miss. Stand-out. As good as it gets. These were some of the sentiments surrounding Baltimore Orioles second baseman Jackson Holliday ahead of his first overall selection in the 2022 MLB Draft. Holliday was heralded. He’d sign an $8.19 million signing bonus to signify such a fact, the largest ever for a high schooler.
Holliday earned every bit of that praise. In 2024, his first full season of professional baseball, the then 19-year-old hit .323/.442/.499 with a .941 OPS, 12 home runs, and 75 RBIs. He’d made Triple-A by season’s end. And by Spring Training of 2025, most hoped Holliday might break camp with the team. He didn’t. Yet faith was high. CBS Sports, in its write-up of Holliday’s dismissal, said, “All of Holliday’s indicators, statistical and otherwise, are neon green.”
Holliday eventually got his promotion. And when he did, no one wavered. ESPN’s Jeff Passan followed the news of his promotion with an addendum: “For those wondering: Yes, the Orioles are still eligible to receive a first-round draft pick via the Prospect Promotion Incentive if Jackson Holliday wins AL Rookie of the Year.” He’d yet to play an MLB game, and baseball’s best insider was already clarifying Holliday’s eligibility to win Rookie of the Year.
Holliday did not win the 2024 AL Rookie of the Year. He didn’t even finish in the top 7. Largely because Holliday couldn’t even finish the season in the Majors. He’d go 2-for-34 10 games into his debut season before his demotion to Triple-A. The light turned yellow. And now it’s bright red. A sharp, unmistakable hue, the color of Mars.
This season, before ending it prematurely due to left wrist inflammation, Holliday hit .229/.300/.340 with a .640 OPS and 81 wRC+. The prospect who once had the highest floor didn’t even come near the play of your average MLB player. What the hell happened?
What happened first, before 2026, was 2025. The season promised to be Holliday’s first full MLB season. He made the Opening Day roster and was penciled in as an everyday infielder. It was go, go, go on the Orioles’ end. They were flashing the checkered flag. Yet Holliday hit just .242 with a .690 OPS and 96 wRC+. The former was the 21st-worst among all 145 qualified hitters in baseball. The latter had Holliday tied for the 31st-worst. What went wrong with Holliday this season is what’s gone wrong in every season: underachievement. It’s as simple as that.
But what’s the cause of this inability? That’s a little trickier to answer.
Perhaps the most obvious of Holliday’s maladies is his problems making contact the way he needs to. This season, Holliday ranked in the 36th and 20th percentile in Barrel Rate and Hard-Hit Rate, respectively. This, well, doesn’t lend itself to success. Nor do Holliday’s previous placements, seeing him rank in the 39th percentile in Barrel Rate and the 40th in Hard-Hit Rate in 2025. His recent woes are the same as the old ones. And to some extent, that’s still shocking.
In 2024, when Holliday had a .908 OPS in 73 Triple-A games, he finished in the 70th percentile in Barrel Rate and the 90th in Hard-Hit Rate, per Prospect Savant. It doesn’t get much better than that. Actually, scratch that. It hasn’t. This is perhaps the most troubling sign. Holliday can’t handle Major League pitching. He can’t drive balls at high speeds. He can’t barrel balls. These are the pillars of success. Even if actual success remains elusive, strong rankings here provide hope. They show a semblance of a tool. But Holliday’s belt is empty.
Among other empty loops is, unsurprisingly, a struggle to hit balls with any real velocity. He ranked in the 18th percentile in Average Exit Velocity this year at 87 MPH, tied for the 45th-slowest in all of baseball. Holliday also doesn’t create any advantages for himself. He’s a little above-average walker with a somehow career-best 9.6% Walk Rate. He’s also striking out more than average, with a 23.7% K Rate, placing him in the 34th percentile. In other words, he doesn’t make loud contact. Nor does he help himself get on base despite that. Instead, he keeps himself off the infield dirt because he’s punching out almost a quarter of the time. He’s sputtering.
Like some rickety Oldsmobile, he also can’t handle top speeds. Against fastballs this season, Holliday is only hitting .263 and slugging .398. And he’s lucky to be doing that well. His xBA against all fastballs is .247, and his xSLG is .377. Even worse, Holliday can’t handle four-seamers most of all. He’s hitting .238 on your standard, non-variety fastball and slugging .366 with a .308 wOBA. That’s despite seeing the pitch 34.9% of the time. The next closest pitch he saw this season is a sinker at 15.7%. In layman’s terms, Holliday is seeing four-seamers twice as often as he’s seeing any other pitch, and he’s still stuck in neutral.
None of these are things that can be wiped away like rain on a windshield wiper. These are the basics. He can’t drive the ball, and he can’t hit four-seam fastballs. It’s a bad match for anyone, let alone the former best prospect in baseball.
The Verdict: Obey the red light. Don’t go. Holliday could be an interesting buy-low dynasty add. He is, after everything, just 22. One can look to July of this year for hope. But August and September brought back that old, shameful shade, and it’s not neon green.
Mickey Moniak, OF, Colorado Rockies
In Colorado Rockies outfielder Mickey Moniak, one could see Holliday’s ghost of Christmas Yet to Come. A former first-overall pick, Moniak himself had high expectations. But like Holliday, he failed to realize them. He’d fizzle out in Philadelphia, get shipped to Los Angeles to play for the Angels in 2022, and be released by them early in 2025. All seemed lost for Moniak. But one day after his release, on March 25, 2025, he’d sign a one-year contract to play with Colorado’s island of misfit toys.
It was here that Moniak finally found his step. In 135 games, Moniak hit .270/.306/.518 with an .824 OPS and 111 wRC+. He’d sock 24 home runs, a new career-best, collect 68 RBIs, another career-high, and 20 doubles. After years in the cold, Moniak seemed to find a home. The chill was gone. The frost stayed thawed in 2026, with Moniak hitting .278/.321/.560, good enough for an .881 OPS and 123 wRC+ in his first 72 games of the season. For his efforts, the Rockies extended him to a two-year, $16.25 million contract extension on August 4.
Everything seemed settled. Moniak seemed salvaged. But over the last 30 games, the old Moniak’s leapt back out like some Jack-in-the-box. Over this last month or so, Moniak’s hit .168/.202/.310. His 22 wRC+ over this span is second-worst in baseball, trailing only Detroit’s Dillon Dingler. Likewise, his .511 OPS is eighth-worst. One of the few players with a worse OPS is Holliday. The present keeps the company of the future. Maybe. We’ll see.
What’s gone wrong for Moniak isn’t much of a mystery. Three ghosts aren’t needed to illuminate his woes. For starters, he’s having very little luck just putting contact on the ball. His BABIP since August 12, eight days after signing his extension, is .222. That’s tied for 19th-worst in all of baseball. Good players can have bad BABIP numbers. It’s not prohibitive. But when in conjunction with a .168 average, well, it doesn’t bode well.
Part of this is Moniak keeping himself from making contact. Earlier this season, he only had a 25.4% K Rate. For a player who’s transitioned to a power-first hitter, it’s not a restrictive number. Over the last 30 games, however, Moniak has a 32.8% K Rate. September is to blame for most of this. Moniak has struck out 18 times in just 51 plate appearances, equating to a 35.3% K Rate. Accompanying this is a 57% Chase Rate in September and a 36.1% Swing & Miss Rate. He’s as blind as Santa without a red-bulbed reindeer.
All of this makes Moniak’s life impossible. He’s set himself as a slugger. That is his part to play. As such, he needs to make just some contact. Instead, he’s making none. It’s costing him not just his average and K Rate but his Barrel Rate, one of the few stats Moniak truly needs to care about. From the start of the season through July, Moniak had a 10.9% Barrel Rate. It’s partly what led him to club 17 homers in his first 17 games. Since August 12, he has a 5.3% Barrel Rate, more than half his previous mark. His ISO has also fallen to the wayside, from .282 through July to .142 over his last 30 games.
Despite all these staggering falls, some freeze seemed destined. Even when Moniak was hot this season, something underneath haunted him like three otherworldly spectres: His expected numbers. Moniak’s xBA over the first half of the season was .226, .052 points worse than his then .278 average. That +.052 difference was the greatest in baseball. That’s not where it ends. The +.131 difference between Moniak’s slugging percentage and his xSLG was also the greatest in baseball. As was the +0.71 difference between his wOBA and xWOBA. No one was luckier than Moniak. Not even a kid on Christmas.
The Verdict: One cannot say humbug here. Moniak, for all his warts past and present, is a no-go. Not unless he re-learns the meaning of Chris– baseball.
Jung Hoo Lee, OF, San Francisco Giants
The San Francisco Giants were desperate for a star heading into the 2023-2024 offseason. The team was aging. Caught between its past and its inevitable future. Something needed to change. The Giants were not ignorant of that. They’d already chased after then-free-agent Bryce Harper in the 2019 offseason. They’d inked Carlos Correa to a megadeal before medicals intervened. And most recently, they’d whiffed on bringing Aaron “Arson” Judge back to the Bay Area. It was miss after miss for a team steadily on the decline.
Perhaps because of all this, the Giants turned their eye across the Pacific. More accurately, towards Kiwoom Heroes outfielder Jung Hoo Lee. San Fran snagged the 2022 KBO MVP and six-time All-Star thanks to a six-year, $113 million contract. Lee was not Harper. Nor was he Correa. He especially wasn’t Judge. But he was a fish reeled in. Something new. Something added.
Three years into Lee’s tenure, the Giants aren’t only closer to escaping purgatory. The team has finished fourth twice and third once. They’ve yet to make the playoffs and have not finished above .500. They are as they were, which is the last thing the Giants, or their fans, wanted. Lee started to be, however. Through his first 88 games of the season, he hit .302/.333/.429, with a .762 OPS and 111 wRC+. He provided an updraft while the air of almost everyone else was headed downstream. It was a fitting change of fate for the Grandson of the Wind.
But the air’s stopped moving. The hits have stopped falling. Since August 15, Lee’s hitting .223/.298/.295 with a .593 OPS and a 68 wRC+. Lee’s OPS and wRC+ over that time are the worst among any qualified Giants hitter. Think about that. The Giants are 14-20 in this time. Their offense is 23rd in runs scored this season. Yet players like Jonah Cox, Turner Hill, and Christian Koss have been more productive and valuable than Lee. It’s as damning as it is telling.
What’s most noticeable about Lee’s play is his decreased power. Before the All-Star Break, Lee had a .429 slugging percentage and a .127 ISO. Five home runs, yes, but 21 doubles and three triples. He got his extra-bases without hitting the ball over the fence. Over his last 31 games, Lee’s slugging .295, down 0.134 points. Of the 168 qualified players in that span, Lee’s slugging percentage is 158th. He has just one home run, five doubles, and an ISO of .071.
Unlike Moniak, this doesn’t have to be crippling. As is evident, Lee is not a power hitter. That’s not his game. For instance, his Barrel Rate and Hard Hit Rate pre-All-Star were 2.3% and 28.3%, respectively. He didn’t, hasn’t, and won’t lend himself to that sort of style. That said, he cannot be one of the least powerful players in the game. He may not need to be a turbine, but being a mill would more than suffice. Instead, he’s a window fan.
More concerning, though, is Lee’s inability to make contact. That is his game. It always has been. He never hit under .300 in any of his seven seasons in the KBO. And in the Majors, he’s always hit above .260. Respectable numbers. As stated before, his batting average during this slump is .223. Of that aforementioned pool of 168 players, that .223 average ranks 133rd. As for BABIP, Lee went from a .322 BABIP, 37th-best in baseball pre-All-Star, to a .240 BABIP. The latter is 144th in baseball.
Stranger than this is how Lee’s replaced his contact. He’s not grounding more balls into the dirt. It’s the opposite. He’s gone from a 45.1% Groundball Rate to 31.7%. He’s also, oddly, got a higher Line Drive Rate now than he did then. It’s gone from 23.9% to 27.7%. It’s up. So, where is Lee putting all his balls? Into the air. He’s gone from a pre-All-Star Fly Ball Rate of 31% to 40.6% over his last 31 games. Jake Bauers has a Fly Ball Rate of 40.8%. Spencer Jones has a 40.9%. Lee should not be sharing the air with them. It’s not who he is.
One more stat showcasing Lee’s misguided change in approach, or happenstance of it, is his Hard Hit Rate. Lee has a Hard-Hit Rate of 39.4% since August 15. It’s 38.2% in August and 36.8% in September. These are not season highs for Lee. These are the highest Hard-Hit Rates he’s had in any month of his entire career. It’s incredibly strange.
Amidst all the turbulence is one steadying patch. Lee is perhaps the most unlucky hitter post-All-Star. His xBA is .282, .046 points higher than his .236 batting average. Only five hitters in all of baseball have been unluckier than Lee in that regard. Five. The hitter of old still exists inside Lee. He may be lost in the sky, but he’s somewhere amongst the clouds.
The Verdict: Watch Lee fly away somewhere else. It’s late in the season. Hitters in this sort of tailspin don’t pull out of it. Especially when an injury’s cut his season short.

item.content:encoded:
New MLB Rumors on Marcelo Mayer's Desire for Red Sox Exit Prior to Giants Trade at Deadline
Marcelo Mayer never lived up to lofty expectations with the Boston Red Sox, and he was apparently happy to be traded away ahead of this year's deadline.
Susan Slusser of the San Francisco Chronicle reported Monday that Mayer and his family were "frustrated" in Boston and "let the Red Sox front office know they'd be comfortable with a trade." They got their wish, as Boston traded him to the San Francisco Giants.
The trade ended a tenure in Boston that started when he was the No. 4 overall pick of the 2021 MLB draft.
However, Slusser noted "fans and sports-talk media soured on him" as he dealt with a variety of setbacks and "gained a reputation for being fragile, an unfair assessment especially because three of his injuries occurred on the field and two others were deemed the result of overwork."
Those injuries included fouling a ball off his foot, hurting his shoulder while running the bases and playing through it, multiple wrist setbacks that eventually required surgery, back concerns, and a forearm stress reaction.
He played just 114 games for the Red Sox and slashed .223/.278/.346 with seven home runs and 32 RBI.
"Obviously, it didn't go the way I wanted, and obviously, outside the lines, it's a lot over there," Mayer said.
The Red Sox have a massive fanbase and generate plenty of attention, which only brought more scrutiny to Mayer's struggles. His father, Enrique Mayer, put things into perspective following the trade.
"In Boston, if you're going well, you're a god and if you're struggling, they're going to tear you apart," he said. "He didn't come out as hot this year and the fans thought he didn't care—that's the most ridiculous thing to say about a major-league baseball player, people don't know the sacrifices and work it takes just to get there. But he got a bad rap and if you get a little bit of one in Boston, it just snowballs."
Mayer now has a fresh start back in his home state of California, although he struck out in each of his four at-bats in Monday's 5-2 loss to the Minnesota Twins in his debut with the Giants.
There will surely be some rust to work through, but he will attempt to live up to the hype and expectations that surrounded him when he was a top-five draft pick as he becomes more experienced with San Francisco.

item.content:encoded:
Pirates' Paul Skenes Explains How World Baseball Classic Held Him Back
Paul Skenes is still Paul Skenes, but the Pittsburgh Pirates superstar right-hander is having a down year by his standards.
What's the core reason for Skenes' 2026 performance? Well, the 2025 National League Cy Young Award winner thinks the 2026 World Baseball Classic "definitely affected the year" and "was kind of the root" of his struggles.
"Usually, that time of year [early March], you’re kind of ramping up and it’s a little bit slow. You can kind of get onto the slope and find your body. One live [batting practice], you’re topping at 97 [mph], and then the next you’re 98, 99. And that wasn’t the case this year. ... Looking back, I don’t think that really helped," Skenes said in an interview with the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette.
Skenes found success in the 2026 World Baseball Classic, which took place from early-to-mid March. Over two starts for Team USA, he recorded a 1.08 ERA, an 0.96 WHIP and nine strikeouts over 8 ⅓ innings pitched, holding opponents to a .226 batting average.
Among the talking points surrounding Skenes this season has been his slight dip in velocity. Granted, his four-seam fastball is still registering in the mid-to-high 90s on the radar gun.
"When you go outing to outing, you don’t really see the big picture sometimes. And I think looking back, I can kind of see it now," Skenes said. "Because early in the season, you can get away with stuff mechanically, or you might not be moving perfectly, but you’re fresh and the velocity is there because you’re feeling good. … You can’t get away with that in July and August and September."
Through 31 starts, Skenes has recorded a 3.91 ERA, a 1.13 WHIP and a 114 ERA+, while totaling 192 strikeouts and 3.1 wins above replacement over 168.0 innings pitched.
For context, Skenes posted an NL-best 1.97 ERA, 0.95 WHIP and 226 ERA+ last year, while totaling 216 strikeouts and eight wins above replacement. In 2025, Skenes gave up 11 home runs. This year, he has surrendered 19 home runs.
Paul Skenes has been an All-Star in each of his three seasons in the sport. (Photo by Daniel Shirey/WBCI/MLB Photos via Getty Images)
Moreover, Skenes posted a 1.96 ERA, an 0.95 WHIP and a 211 ERA+ over 23 starts in his 2024 rookie campaign (133.0 innings pitched), while racking up 170 strikeouts, 5.8 wins above replacement and finishing third in NL Cy Young Award voting.
"Stuff changes over the course of the season and from outing to outing. With that said, there’s been a lot more changes, outing to outing this year, that I kind of just don’t have an answer for body-wise," Skenes expressed.
Skenes and the Pirates are 79-77. While eliminated from playoff contention, Pittsburgh has the chance to post its first winning season since 2018.

item.content:encoded:
Dodgers minor league center fielder Alek Thomas on Monday was named Pacific Coast League player of the week for the final week of the regular season, after a strong five games for Triple-A Oklahoma City.
Thomas joined teammate Jackson Ferris, who won pitcher of the week for last week.
Thomas had nine hits in 17 at-bats on the road at El Paso last week with two triples, two doubles, and four walks, hitting .529/.636/.882 with six runs scored, four RBI, and one stolen base. He finished off his season with four consecutive multi-hit games.
Thomas played five years for the Arizona Diamondbacks before getting designated for assignment in May. The Dodgers acquired him on May 12 for minor league outfielder Jose Requena. Thomas hit .305/.378/.537 with 36 extra-base hits in 68 games for Oklahoma City, his 131 wRC+ his best in the minors since 2021.
In seven games for the Dodgers, Thomas had four hits in 19 at-bats with a double and three runs batted in. He was designated for assignment on September 5, and is no longer on the 40-man roster.
Eight Oklahoma City Comets won Pacific Coast League player or pitcher of the week this season — James Tibbs (March 31—April 5 and May 25-31), Alex Freeland (May 11-17), Jack Suwinski (June 9-14), Ryder Ryan (June 9-14), Emmet Sheehan (August 17-23), Cole Irvin (September 7-13), Jackson Ferris, and Thomas.
Oklahoma City plays for the Pacific Coast League championship in a best-of-3 series beginning Tuesday night on the road against the Las Vegas Aviators, an A's affiliate.

item.title: [FanSided] Bobby Witt Jr. reveals what went wrong in the Royals 'disappointing' 2026 season
item.dc:creator: John Perrotto

However, the Royals’ postseason run, which included upsetting the Baltimore Orioles in an American League Wild Card Series, seems like eons ago. The Royals ar
item.content:encoded:
The future couldn’t have looked better for the Kansas City Royals in 2024. They had one of baseball’s brightest young stars in Bobby Witt Jr. and reached the postseason for the first time in nine years.
Two years later, the Royals still have Witt and the 26-year-old three-time All-Star shortstop remains one of baseball’s top young players. However, the Royals’ postseason run, which included upsetting the Baltimore Orioles in an American League Wild Card Series, seems like eons ago.
The Royals are 67-89 going into their final six games and are likely to finish last in the AL Central. That is quite a drop from their 86-76 record two years ago and even their 82-80 mark of last season.
Witt isn’t going anywhere. He is signed through 2030 and there are player and team options from 2031-37 in Witt’s seven-year, $148.78-million contract.
Bobby Witt Jr. and the Royals aren't heading in the right direction
Witt’s career continues to ascend as his 6.5 bWAR this season is third in the AL behind New York Yankees right-hander Cam Schlittler (7.0) and Detroit Tigers rookie infielder Kevin McGonigle (6.7). Witt is hitting .279/.359/.440 with 18 home runs and 43 stolen bases in 137 games.
Yet the Royals are descending as they have the fifth-worst record in the major leagues. It’s hard not to think that the franchise is beginning to waste a golden opportunity while having Witt under contract.
| Team | Win % |
|---|---|
| Royals | .429 |
| Giants | .414 |
| Athletics | .391 |
| Angels | .385 |
| Rockies | .365 |
Witt is obviously disappointed with the way this season has played out. However, he is not the type of person who is going to publicly going to criticize the organization or tell president of baseball operations J.J. Piccolo how to do his job.
“I think we need some pieces, which you can tell from looking at our record,” Witt told FanSided. “But I know for me personally and most of the guys that the season has been disappointing in the sense that it hasn’t come close to turning out like we wanted it to just because we didn't perform the way we wanted to. We felt like we had the team to go where we wanted to go in spring training and coming into the season.”
The last time the Royals were over .500 was on April Fools Day when they beat the visiting Minnesota Twins 13-9 at Kauffman Stadium to improve to 3-2. An eight-game losing streak from April 12-20 dropped the Royals to 7-16 and they’ve never recovered despite having a nine-game winning streak in August.
“We just got away from playing good baseball this year,” Witt said. “We just need to get back to playing our game, not overthinking things and just doing the little things that can make us a good team.
“I think it's just kind of make sure we're just focused each and every day, focus on our work, and that the emphasis has to be on doing whatever we can to win each night’s game.”
The Royals have not been good on either side of the ball. They are 24th in MLB in runs scored with 4.21 per game and 25th in runs allowed with a 4.86 average.
Why Bobby Witt Jr. shoulders the blame for Royals tough season
Though Witt ranks among the AL leaders in bWAR, he is not happy about his season and takes his share of the responsibility for the lost season.
“It’s one of those things where you learn a lot about who you are individually and how you can become better,” Witt said. “I feel like that's something to take away from this year. Learn how to kind of be more mentally sound throughout the entire year going through the bumps and bruises throughout a long season and trying to get better every day.”
The Royals, though, do not plan to rebuild this upcoming winter. Piccolo signaled that the Royals plan to contend next season at this year’s trade deadline when he surprisingly rebuffed offers for veteran right-hander Michael Wacha, who has one year remaining on his contract.
Witt is one of four players in the lineup who is 26 or younger, giving the Royals potentially the foundation of a good team. Catcher Carter Jensen’s 25 home runs are a franchise single season record for a rookie. Right fielder Jac Caglianone has 23 homers, 71 RBIs and a team-leading .821 OPS. Though his season has been ruined by a torn hamstring, third baseman Maikel Garcia was an All-Star last year.
“All you ever want is to play in the postseason and it was so much fun two years ago,” Witt said. “To kind of take a step back from that, you get frustrated. You also got to learn from it, build from it and just know that there's a lot of work to do to get back to that position.”

item.title: [CBS Sports] Toughest players to rank at third base for 2027: Jose Ramirez's decline creates a major Fantasy dilemma
item.dc:creator: Chris Towers
item.description: Third base wasn't viewed as a strong position entering 2026, and it doesn't look much stronger. Sure, we had players like Sal Stewart, Miguel Vargas, and Kevin McGonigle breaking out and establishing themselves as the next generation of the position, perhaps, and that ain't nothing. But we also had deeply disappointing seasons from Jose Ramirez, Jazz Chisholm, Manny Machado, Austin Riley, Maikel Garcia, Bo Bichette, Eugenio Suarez, and Noelvi Marte, all of whom were drafted in the top 10 at the
item.content:encoded:
Third base wasn't viewed as a strong position entering 2026, and it doesn't look much stronger. Sure, we had players like Sal Stewart, Miguel Vargas, and Kevin McGonigle breaking out and establishing themselves as the next generation of the position, perhaps, and that ain't nothing.
But we also had deeply disappointing seasons from Jose Ramirez, Jazz Chisholm, Manny Machado, Austin Riley, Maikel Garcia, Bo Bichette, Eugenio Suarez, and Noelvi Marte, all of whom were drafted in the top 10 at the position. It would not be an overstatement to say that eight of the top 10 at the position busted, and you can throw Matt Chapman (3B12 in ADP) and Addison Barger (3B14) in there, too, to round it out.
So, yeah, we needed the breakouts. Because a lot of the old standbys let us down and it's not like the breakouts are without their flaws or concerns – any player who has only done it once is going to enter the next season with at least some question marks. Looking ahead to 2027, Junior Caminero might be the only sure thing at the position. He's going to be a first-rounder no matter what, but if you're the type to play position scarcity games, you might need to make sure you reach for him no matter where you're picking. Because if not, you're going to be left with a big question mark at an important position.
The toughest players to rank at third base
Jose Ramirez, Guardians
There are those who will argue Ramirez is very easy to rank. Some will say you should take his decline at face value; when a 34-year-old starts to fall off, they don't generally get it back. Ramirez enters the final week of the season hitting .237, his worst mark since 2015, while his 12 homers are his fewest since 2016. Sure, there was a mid-season hand surgery to blame it on, but to reiterate an earlier point: You probably shouldn't expect a 34-year-old to be healthier than he was in the past. Just take the numbers and the decline at face value.
That's one approach you can take. But I don't think it'll be mine. Because, despite the mediocre production, it doesn't actually look like Ramirez's skill set has declined much at all. His strikeout rate is up, but at 12.9%, it's still within a percentage point of his career mark, while his walk rate is actually his highest since 2021. His .306 wOBA is his worst mark since 2015, but his .329 expected wOBA is basically right in line with what he did in 2024, when he hit 39 homers and had arguably his best season ever. It's down from 2025, but not so much that it looks like a total collapse of the skill set. Ramirez still makes a ton of contact and he still hits the ball in the air to the pull side as often as anyone, the primary way he has overcome middling quality of contact metrics throughout his career.
Now, I'll grant that it's possible that the small, almost imperceptible changes in Ramirez's underlying skills have more impact than you might expect. Ramirez has been an outlier in how he outruns his underlying metrics, but that can be a delicate dance to keep up; Marcus Semien was an elite Fantasy player with a very similar skill set right up until the point he lost it. The margin for error with this kind of skill set might just be narrower than for guys who can crush the ball consistently, so maybe Ramirez's decline won't be stopped by a healthy offseason.
I'm open to that. He won't be a top-five player in my overall rankings for 2027. But he'll definitely still be a top-five third baseman, and might still be the second option off the board for me.
Miguel Vargas, White Sox
I don't think it's tough to figure out where Vargas ranks among third basemen. He belongs no lower than fourth, and I think you can make an extremely compelling case that only Junior Caminero should be ahead of him. So this might be more about just making sure everyone is prepared for the possibility that Vargas will be a second-round pick in 2027. The level he has reached in 2026 is completely unprecedented for Vargas, who has been playing pretty regularly since the second half of 2024 and had never really shown this kind of difference-making upside. But his .366 wOBA is actually a mild underperformance relative to his .381 expected wOBA, which is actually tied for the fifth-best mark of any hitter in the league.
I don't think Vargas is actually a top-five hitter in baseball. But if you wanted to argue he was a top-10 Fantasy option after this season, I wouldn't have a strong argument against it; the best argument I could muster is just, "Well, he's only done it once." But in addition to the underlying numbers, here's the other thing I love about what we're seeing from Vargas: He just refuses to slow down. July was the worst month of his season, but he responded with a .948 OPS in August, and then he went out and won AL Player of the Week last week. He's hitting .260/.373/.467 in the second half with strong plate discipline and plenty of speed and power.
Those gaudy underlying numbers are a little worse than they were early in the season, which might portend some regression in 2027. But, again, it probably wouldn't be reasonable to expect him to be a top-10 hitter again. But that doesn't mean the breakout isn't real, and where you rank him among Ramirez and Sal Stewart will mostly come down to personal preference. I imagine all three will be at least top-30 picks for me.
Manny Machado, Padres
There was a period in 2026 where Machado looked like himself again, and I was ready to write his slow start off as just that. He started hitting for real power again in June, and then in July he hit .292/.369/.552, putting the miserable start to the season behind him. But despite hitting three homers in his first five games back from the All-Star break, Machado enters the final week with just nine homers in 59 games since the break, while hitting .242/.331/.388 in the second half overall. If he deserved some benefit of the doubt for the slow start, it's hard to keep extending that when he came crashing back to earth over the final two months.
Machado's .330 xwOBA is definitely better than his actual .311 mark. However, it's still his worst since Statcast tracking began, and unlike Ramirez, he doesn't have a consistent track record of overcoming his underlying stats. There's still room for some improvement in 2027, most notably with his batting average, as a .234 BABIP isn't likely to sustain. But if he hits to his .244 xBA instead, that's still a drag on your average. Think about it this way: How excited have you been to have Nolan Arenado in your lineup this season? He hasn't been awful, but he hasn't been worth near the kind of price we've gotten used to paying for Machado. Neither is Machado at this point.
Kazuma Okamoto, Blue Jays
It's been an extremely successful first major-league season for Okamoto, though not necessarily in the way anyone expected. Okamoto was supposed to bring a contact-forward skill set, with just enough power to be a potential all-around impact hitter. Instead, he's been a pretty all-or-nothing power bat, hitting .235/.310/.459 with 33 homers and 89 RBI heading into the second half of the season. A longtime elite contact hitter in Japan, Okamoto has struck out 29% of the time and posted a 14% swinging-strike rate, both bottom-15 marks among qualifiers.
The strikeout issues got a little better in the second half, though he was a sub-.700 OPS bat in July and August before getting really hot in September, so it's hard to argue there's too much momentum building here. It's not unreasonable to expect a bit better from Okamoto with a full season under his belt, but the swing and miss issues on display were worrisome enough that he might just never get past it. Draft him for what he did in 2026, and if you get a .260 average from him instead, that'll be a huge win. But there are enough red flags in this profile that there's a real risk he'll end up being exposed before long.
Curtis Mead, Red Sox
Mead comes with all the typical questions of a one-season breakout, except he didn't even get the chance to do it for a full season. He platooned for part of the early part of the season and then suffered a fractured wrist in his very first game after being traded to the Red Sox in July. When he played, he was terrific, putting up a .253/.353/.498 line and more than holding his own against righties, so the case is pretty similar to that of Vargas as a former top prospect who finally made good. Only he did it for about half as many plate appearances, which makes it inherently more difficult to trust. I mean, just look at Michael Busch, who fully broke out in 2025 and had the underlying data to back it up, but then regressed badly in 2026. That doesn't mean the same thing will happen to Mead (or to Vargas, for that matter), but there's real regression risk that should keep his price down. I still think Mead deserves to be ranked as a top-10 third baseman, but I don't think he'll be worth drafting until at least the double-digit rounds.
Zack Gelof, Athletics
This feels like we're all Charlie Brown and we're gonna run up and try to kick that football again. Gelof has had a pretty awesome season, hitting 19 homers and stealing 14 bases in 105 games, while putting up a very solid .252/.314/.456 line. He has cut his strikeout rate to 25%, the best mark of his career, and while his underlying numbers don't quite back it up, his home park in Sacramento could help explain why it might not be unsustainable.
But we did this with Gelof after his rookie season. We overlooked scary plate discipline and swing-and-miss issues because he was a young, exciting hitter with a power-speed combo, and that was worth betting on. And I'm just not sure I want to make that mistake again. He's a pretty good athlete, but that doesn't really translate into much more than above-average raw power, and I just don't have much faith that's enough to overcome what are still some pretty scary issues under the hood. Gelof has, to his credit, become a more patient hitter, though not necessarily a more discerning one; his chase rate has dropped about as much as his in-zone swing rate has. He still has big swing-and-miss issues, and it just always feels like Gelof is going to be dancing on a knife's edge. If he's still there after the first 150 picks or so, I might be willing to take a chance on him. I just don't think I can bring myself to rank Gelof as a starting-caliber player in most leagues.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Tigers Get Encouraging First Look at Key Piece From Tarik Skubal Trade
item.dc:creator: Laura Lambert; Unknown
item.description: The season is nearly over for the Detroit Tigers, given that they won’t be partaking in any postseason action. That means the final week of baseball is full of evaluations of players who could make or break 2027. Monday evening, the organization and Tigers fans got a great look at an intriguing player. item.content:encoded:
The season is nearly over for the Detroit Tigers, given that they won’t be partaking in any postseason action. That means the final week of baseball is full of evaluations of players who could make or break 2027.
Monday evening, the organization and Tigers fans got a great look at an intriguing player.
River Ryan took the mound and made his Tigers debut against the Washington Nationals. He delivered three scoreless innings in Detroit’s 9-2 victory.
Ryan allowed two hits and one walk while also striking out three. As a piece of the Tarik Skubal trade with the Los Angeles Dodgers, this is encouraging to all involved.
What makes it even better is that it is a chance that is paying off. He hasn’t been on the Major League field for more than two years.
River Ryan Returns
August 10, 2024 was the last time Ryan took the mound before he had to undergo Tommy John surgery.
He missed all of 2025 while recovering and then had to deal with hamstring issues that slowed his return this year. He made two short starts at Triple-A Toledo and then the Tigers decided to give him a chance at the big leagues during the final homestand of the season.
Given how the Tigers acquired Ryan, he has been on the radar for everyone to see how it would work out. He came along with Zyir Hope and Brady Smith when Skubal was traded to the Dodgers.
Everyone knew that finding an immediate replacement for Skubal was an impossible task. Evaluating the value of trade pieces should and will take years rather than weeks.
Monday was an early glance at one of those pieces and Ryan didn’t disappoint.
He kept Washington at bay before he turned things over the Keider Montero who went on to add four scoreless innings of his own.
Detroit’s offense also awakened. Javier Baez, Ben Malgeri and Spencer Torkelson all homered.
Ryan Could Be Very Important
Ryan isn’t a replacement for Skubal, and he isn’t going to prove everything all at once in the final week of the 2026 season.
He is healthy and can make an impression on the organization toward constructing the 2027 rotation.
The Tigers gave him the chance on the Major League mound, and Ryan took the opportunity to show off. The team got an initial look at him against big-league hitters, while Ryan is getting the chance to take some education into the offseason about things to improve.
Trading Skubal was a huge decision for this ballclub, maybe the biggest it has faced in years. Three innings won’t show anyone much about the return Detroit got, but Monday was a good start for Ryan.
After two years away, Ryan found his way back to the mound, and he gave the Tigers an encouraging look at what might be in 2027.
Laura Lambert resides in Wiggins, Colo. with her husband, Ricky and two sons, Brayden and Boedy. She attended the University of Northern Colorado while studying economics. She is an accomplished rodeo athlete and barrel horse trainer along with being a life-long sports fan. Over the years, Laura has been active in journalism in a variety of roles. While continuing to cover western sports and country music, she is currently enjoying expanding her reach into multiple sports including MLB, NFL, and WNBA. Laura covers the Washington Nationals, Houston Astros, Texas Rangers, Detroit Tigers, Colorado Rockies, Toronto Blue Jays, and Rodeo for On SI. You can reach her at lauralambertmedia@gmail.com

Burnes is expected to start a game during the final series of the regular season against the Padres, Alex Weiner of Arizona Sports reports.
Burnes was roughed up by the Yankees on Sunday, allowing four runs on five hits, including three home runs. The right-hander has allowed five home runs and four walks over 10.1 innings since being activated off the injured list. Burnes is pleased with his secondary offerings, but the velocity of his signature pitch, the cutter, is down and not creating enough separation. He's tentatively scheduled to start Saturday.

item.content:encoded:
A new wild statistical club has been created in the big leagues, thanks to Baltimore Orioles slugger Pete Alonso.
The star first baseman hit not one, but two home runs in Baltimore’s 4-3 victory to open their series against the Toronto Blue Jays on Monday at Camden Yards in Baltimore, Md.
With those home runs, he reached the 40-HR plateau in a season for the fourth time in his career — and for the first time since he took his talents to the American League.
According to OptaSTATS, Alonso also became the first player in big-league history to record at least 40 dingers in each of his first seasons in different leagues.
During his rookie season with the New York Mets in 2019, Alonso launched 53 home runs to lead the majors and won the National League Rookie of the Year Award.
With five more games left in the 2026 regular season, Alonso can add to his home run total.
Baltimore is scheduled to face the Blue Jays in the second game of the series on Tuesday, with Toronto sending future Baseball Hall of Famer Max Scherzer to the mound.
For what it’s worth, Alonso is just 4-for-24 with zero home runs against Scherzer in his career, but it might be his lucky day.
